ARTHUR H. WEISS
Grand Master
October 11, 2020–October 10, 2021

ii

ARTHUR H. WEISS
Grand Master
2020–2021
Worshipful Brother Arthur Harold Weiss was raised a Master Mason
in Conejo Valley Lodge No. 807 in Thousand Oaks on January 28, 1986. He
served as Master of the lodge in 1991 and 2003. In 1997, Conejo Valley Lodge
presented him with the Hiram Award for his continued and distinguished
service to the lodge
Brother Weiss has served the Grand Lodge of California as an Inspector,
Grand Marshal and Grand Chaplain. He was Inspector for seven years and
was appointed Grand Marshal in 2004 and Grand Chaplain in 2007. He served
on the Leadership Development Committee for four years and was ViceChairman in 2008-2009. Additionally, he has been a member of the Public
Schools Advisory Council since 2011. Rounding out his service to Grand Lodge,
Brother Weiss has been a trustee of the California Masonic Foundation since
2005, and was President from 2009-2015 and is currently serving as Chairman
of the Board.
In addition to this service, Brother Weiss is active in the concordant and
appendant bodies. He is a member of Signet Chapter No. 57 and Oxnard Chapter
No. 86, Royal Arch Masons, Omega Council No. 11 Cryptic Masons, and Los
Angeles Commandery No. 9 Knights Templar. He served as Grand Orator of
the Grand Council of Cryptic Masons of California in 2008-2009. He received
the 32° in the Scottish Rite Valley of Los Angeles. He has been a member of the
Al Malaikah Shriners since 1998. Brother Weiss is a member of Conejo Valley
Chapter No. 632 and Dr. Rob Morris Chapter No. 651, Order of the Eastern Star.
He is a Past Patron and served as Worthy Grand Patron of the Grand Chapter
of California in 2012-2013. Brother Weiss is also a member of the Southern
California Past Masters Association, Allied Masonic Degrees, Knight Masons,
Red Cross of Constantine, Rosicrucians, and Hi Twelve International.
Brother Weiss received a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Engineering in
1973 from Purdue University. In 1976, he joined Rocketdyne beginning a 42-year
career in aerospace. He managed many aspects of aerospace technology including work on the Space Shuttle Main Engines, Shuttle flight operations, advanced
launch systems, and missile defense programs. In 1996, he led development of
the RS-68 engine for the Delta IV launch vehicle. He was promoted to Program
Director of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense in 2002 and then Director of
iii

Altitude Control Propulsion Systems in 2008. In 2012, he became Director of
Advanced Programs. During his tenure Art received many professional designations and awards of recognition, including a Rocketdyne President’s Award
for the first Shuttle launch and the NASA Distinguished Service Award. He
retired in 2015.
Art and his wife, Barbara Jean, live in Newbury Park and have one adult
daughter, Lauren Weiss Stolkin.

ONE HUNDRED SEVENTY SECOND
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION

Friday Afternoon, October 8, 2021
The Grand Lodge officers serving in 2019-20 processed into the Grand Lodge,
and Most Worshipful Brother John E. Trauner, Past Grand Master, expressed
his sincere thanks to Grand Master Arthur H. Weiss for the opportunity share
this moment with the Grand Lodge, as he and the other 2019-20 Grand Lodge
officers were unable to do so due to the COVID-19 pandemic, as the 171st Annual
Communication was held virtually.
Worshipful Brother Lee M. Wilbourne, Master of Nevada Lodge No. 13,
raised the Grand Lodge for the first time in the opening session using a handmade pinecone gavel presented to Grand Master Trauner by Worshipful Brother
Mike Mavrakis.
The 2019-2020 Grand Lodge Officers retired from the auditorium. The
2020-2021 Grand Lodge Offices processed in.
The 172nd Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master Arthur
H. Weiss on Friday, October 8, 2021.
Worshipful Brother Brien S. Lynch, Master of Conejo Valley Lodge No.
807, raised the Grand Lodge during the opening session using Mjolnir, a gavel
presented to the Grand Master by Sister Sarahann Shapiro, Past Grand Matron
of the Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, on the occasion of
his installation as Grand Master the prior year. The Grand Master noted that he
would make use of that gavel, together with a smaller version of the same gavel,
as well as a gavel he commissioned from Worshipful Brother Chris L. Holme, a
Past Master of the Downtown Masonic Lodge No. 859, and presented to Sister
Sarahann at their installation as Worthy Grand Matron and Worthy Grand
Patron of the Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star in 2013.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand Marshal
to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at the Altar.

6

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, and the Grand
Master and Deputy Grand Master personally greeted each one. The Grand
Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our Past Grand Masters by
the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters were then escorted
to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master then directed
the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the usual letter
of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain whether a constitutional number was present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The
following were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

The Grand Secretary announced that, according to the Credentials Report, there
were 685 Master Masons registered as of 12 p.m. Friday, with at least 20 percent
of the lodges chartered by this Grand Lodge represented, and that therefore a
quorum was present as required for the transaction of business.
The Grand Secretary reported that all lodges have paid their annual per
capita assessment to Grand Lodge.
Grand Lodge Opening
The Grand Master then opened Grand Lodge in ancient form. The Grand
Marshal and the Deacons retired to escort the flag of the United States of
America into the auditorium, which was followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.
Introductions
The following were asked to rise as groups for recognition:
Residents of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek, Diamond Jubilee
Award recipients, Golden Veteran Award recipients, Hiram Award recipients,
Worshipful Masters, Lodge Secretaries and Officers, Constitutional Board
Members, Grand Lodge Committeemen, and District Inspectors; each group
was greeted with a round of applause.
The Grand Master also recognized Grand Lodge Officers visiting from
other jurisdictions.
Reception of Visiting Grand Masters
The Grand Master then directed the Grand Marshal to escort the visiting Grand
Masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The following were
received with Private Grand Honors and introduced:

Legislation
The Grand Master called on the Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee, Most
Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, Past Grand Master, for his report (Appendix K).
The Grand Master then called on the Chairman of the Finance Committee,
Worshipful Levon H. Keshishian, for his report (Appendix K).
The Grand Master instructed the members of the established rules governing the proper protocol and manner of discussion on the various pieces of
legislation and proceeded with the legislation starting with Grand Master’s
Recommendations.

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Mark J. McNee, Grand
Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren. His
remarks were as follows:

14

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

I am sorry for your losses. The pandemic compelled us to become creative
in the ways we have traditionally gathered, the way we grieve, and the way we
say goodbye. For a time we were unable to assemble in the character of Masons
and with the solemn formalities of our Craft, to offer up to their memory, before
the world, the last tribute of our affection.
For this segment of our annual communication, this candle represents
our lost friends, family members, brothers, and mentors. May it represent the
light they sought in their travels in Masonry, and may it remind us of the light,
warmth, and joy our dearly departed brought to each of our lives.
In the presence of death, we are reminded of our mortality. There are so
many lessons to be taken from our collective recent experience. When thinking
of the departed, what are the legacies and lessons that they left for us? And
having known them, and learned so much from them, what legacies and lessons
will we leave for future generations? I hope that in the face of our mortality
we will be more humble and grateful, more present in life’s precious fleeting
moments, and that we will endeavor to imitate and improve upon the legacies
and lessons exemplified by the departed.
We read in the Holy Writings from 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5, Verse 1, “For
we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building
from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.” This verse is
so familiar to us as Masons, and in it Paul describes our bodies in this world as
a temporary dwelling place, like a tent. It is not meant to last forever. We are
not meant to be here forever. But waiting in eternity is a dwelling place that will
last forever. Far better than any house on earth, for it is not made with human
hands, it is provided for by the Lord.
And while the departed have left these earthly toils for that spiritual house,
we will never forget the light, warmth, and joy they brought to us. We will never
forget their legacies and lessons. For a true mentor never really dies—their
work lives on in you.
As we continue to live out our days, do so enriched by having known the
deceased as a loving sibling, parent, grandparent, friend, brother, or mentor.
Look beyond the grief of today and recall your most joyous memories of the
deceased, and live your lives to the fullest, to the benefit of those around you,
as they would have wished you to do. And when we are next presented with a
reminder of our mortality, let us think about the legacies and lessons we will
leave for future generations, just as our dearly departed did in their time on
this earth.
It is now my honor to provide a eulogy of our late Grand Bible Bearer,
Worshipful Frank Young.
Worshipful Frank Rickey Young was born in Santa Cruz on January 24, 1946,
and later attended Santa Cruz High School and Soquel High School, where he
was in the first graduating class in 1963. Worshipful Frank joined DeMolay and
was part of a group of DeMolays invited to become the first corps of officers for
the Northern California DeMolay Association, which provided his introduction

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

15

to the world of Masonry, where he would enjoy a lifetime of true friendship.
Worshipful Frank attended Cabrillo College and was a graduate of San José
State University. He worked many years in Santa Cruz, first as vice president
of finance for the Santa Cruz Seaside Company, and later in his own certified
public accounting practice for 30 years.
Worshipful Frank was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason in April 1967
in Santa Cruz-San Lorenzo Valley No. 38, and was raised to the sublime degree
of Master Mason in February 1968.
In addition to his Masonic journey, Worshipful Frank loved the Order of the
Eastern Star and was a Past Patron of Wild Lily Chapter and a Past Grand Patron
of California. He was also involved in the York Rite, Scottish Rite, Shriners, and
the Royal Order of Scotland.
Worshipful Frank served as Master of Santa Cruz-San Lorenzo Valley No.
38 in 1981 and served as Secretary of Confidence No. 110 from 2006 until his
passing. He served with distinction in many other roles, including as Candidates
Coach, Trustee, and Assistant Secretary at his beloved Santa Cruz lodges.
It is often said that a secretary of a lodge often stays in place for many years
and becomes a staple of that lodge, and there is no doubt Worshipful Frank was
that man at Confidence No. 110.
Worshipful Frank received the Hiram Award from Confidence No. 110 in
October 2007, and received his Golden Veteran Award for 50 years of membership in our Fraternity in June 2018, again at Confidence No. 110.
Worshipful Frank served the Grand Lodge of California as a member and
Vice Chair of the Grand Lodge Audit Committee and in numerous roles for the
Nob Hill Masonic Center.
Worshipful Frank served as the 2020-21 Grand Bible Bearer of the Grand
Lodge of California up until he entered into rest at the age of 75 on May 27, 2021,
from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (commonly known as ALS), which is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that affects nerve cells in the brain and the
spinal cord. Worshipful Frank is survived by his beloved wife of 55 years, Kathy
Young, their daughter Kristan Dunston, son Chris Young, and five grandchildren.
Into your hands O Lord we commend our Brother Frank.

Leo B. Mark

Grand Master 1987-1988
San Jose No. 10
May 6, 1922 – September 27, 2020

EULOGY
LEO B. MARK
Most Worshipful Leo Bon Mark entered into the Celestial Lodge on September
27, 2020. He was a local Bay Area product. Our Grand Master, the first of Chinese
ancestry to serve as such, was born on May 6, 1922 in San Francisco, California.
Leo attended public schools here in San Francisco and continued his education at San José State University, where he earned a bachelor’s degree. He served
his country in the United States Army during World War II in 1944 and 1945.
Leo’s career in law enforcement was with the Santa Clara County district
attorney’s office, from which he retired as chief investigator.
On May 21, 1944, he married the charming and petite Lora Moy, who passed
away on April 7, 2000, and from this union five children were born—two boys
and three girls.
Most Worshipful Leo was raised a Master Mason on August 15, 1955 in San
Jose Lodge No. 10.
Leo served our Grand Lodge and Masonry for over 50 years. After serving
as Master of San Jose No. 10 in 1964, Leo went on to serve as Inspector from
1966 through 1975 and Grand Sword Bearer for the 1975-76 Grand Lodge year.
He had also served on numerous committees and boards prior to his election
to the progressive line.
Most Worshipful Leo served with honor as the 122nd Grand Master of
California and Hawaii in 1987-88. He has the distinction of being the last Grand
Master to serve both jurisdictions at the same time.
Most Worshipful Leo was also active in Scottish Rite. He served the San
Jose Valley as Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection, Commander of the
Council of Kadosh, and Master of Kadosh of the Consistory. He also served as
President of the San Jose Scottish Rite Foundation. Leo was honored with the
rank of decoration of Honorary Inspector General of the 33º in 1975. After his
term as Grand Master, Most Worshipful Leo served as Personal Representative
of the Sovereign Grand Inspector General in San Jose for 17 years.
Leo was a member of Islam Shriners (now Asiya), and he and Lora were
members of Campbell Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star.
Leo was also a recipient of the Honorary Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay.
Most Worshipful Leo was active in community service, being a charter
President of the Chinese American Citizens’ League of Santa Clara County, a
Past President of the San Jose Chinese Language School, a Past President of
the California District Attorney Investigators’ Association, and a member of
the Advisory Board of the Santa Clara County Valley Police Academy.
He will be remembered for his leadership, dignity, kindness, graciousness,
compassion, fairness and, when appropriate, a sense of humor. His thoughts and
actions were always for the benefit of the Craft and the image of Freemasonry.
He was a quiet individual but was aware of everything around him.
He will be sadly missed by all. Until we meet again—farewell, my brother.

The Grand Master thanked Most Worshipful Brother Loui and called

EULOGY
C. RAY WHITAKER
Most Worshipful Clarence Ray Whitaker was born on October 18, 1931 in Madera,
California. His family were pioneers and one of the founding families of the
City of Madera. From an early age he was called C. Ray or just Ray. He attended
public schools in Madera, and upon graduating from Madera Union High School
in 1950, he joined the United States Air Force. He served from 1950 to 1953,
during the Korean conflict, as a staff and supply sergeant. Upon completion of
his enlistment, he returned to his beloved Madera and made it his home for
the rest of his life.
In July 15, 1952, C. Ray married his childhood sweetheart Joyce Parker. They
were happily married for the next 70 years. They raised two sons and were
blessed with three granddaughters and one grandson. They were both active
members in the First Christian Church in Madera.
Upon returning from the Air Force, C. Ray joined his father in the family
business, Whitaker’s Auto Wrecking, and soon took over running it for nearly
50 years. He was active in his community, working with many organizations to
make it a better place to live. He was a volunteer crossing guard and a volunteer
assistant reading teacher for the Madera School District. He worked with the
Chamber of Commerce, Madera Rescue Mission, Veterans of Foreign Wars
Post No. 1981, Madera County Historical Society, Camp Fire Girls, and Boy
Scouts of America, to name only a few. He stayed active in scouting after his
kids became adults and served Madera Troop No. 116 as scout master for many
years. With more than 50 years of service in scouting, he was honored with the
Silver Beaver Award and the Daniel Carter Beard Masonic Scouter Award from
the Grand Lodge of California.
C. Ray began his Masonic journey in March of 1957 in Madera Lodge No.
280. He served as its Master for the first time in 1965. Then served Joppa Lodge
No. 508 as its Master three times and Madera Lodge as its Master four more
times, with the last time in 2015. C. Ray received the Hiram Award from his
lodge in 1982 and his Fifty-Year Pin in 2007. He was very active in his lodge and
was still mentoring and serving as an officer when he passed away.
C. Ray joined the York Rite, Tehran Shrine, and Fresno Scottish Rite. He
was active in Scottish Rite for more than 50 years, holding many offices, and
for 20 years performed in the degrees. He received his KCCH in 1983 and was
coroneted a 33º Inspector General Honorary in 1993. He was the Personal
Representative for SGIG in Fresno for six years in the 1990s.
C. Ray belonged to the Sciots, National Sojourners, Royal Order of Scotland,
Robert the Bruce Association, Southern California Research Lodge, Scottish Rite

20

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Research Society, Masonic Origins Research Lodge in Clovis, and High Twelve
Club. He and Joyce were both members of the Madera Chapter Order of the
Eastern Star, and C. Ray served twice as Worthy Patron.
He was an adult leader for the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls
and the International Order of DeMolay. He was a Rainbow Dad for his local
Assembly and an adviser for the DeMolay Chapter. He received the Legion of
Honor from DeMolay International.
He served the Grand Lodge of California as an Inspector for seven years
until was appointed the Grand Sword Bearer by Most Worshipful Roy J. Henville,
Past Grand Master, in 1984. He then served four years as the Grand Tiler, until
he was appointed Grand Marshall by Most Worshipful Sam Pavlovich in 1989.
C. Ray served on various Youth Orders and Membership Development committees. He served the Masonic Hospital Visitors Program for many years. C.
Ray also served as a director for the Nob Hill Masonic Center, as a trustee for
the California Masonic Temple, California Masonic Foundation, and Masonic
Homes of California.
C. Ray was elected Junior Grand Warden in 1998 and continued up the
Grand Lodge line to be elected and installed as the Grand Master of Masons
in California on October 10, 2001. His theme was “Communication: Key to
Education.” He worked diligently to lay the groundwork to improve Masonic
education and encourage Masonic research across California. His term as Grand
Master began in the shadow of 9/11. He led the effort in California to raise funds
in support of the Grand Lodge of New York’s appeal to help the families of the
first responders killed on that tragic day. California raised over $100,000 during
his term as Grand Master.
C. Ray traveled all around the state during his year, visiting lodges and
Masonic organizations, delivering his message of Masonic education and leadership. He laid 30 cornerstones during his term, including 25 at a public school
or government building. He worked tirelessly to raise awareness of our beloved
Fraternity around the state and encouraged lodges to be a force for good in
their communities.
C. Ray was loved by one and all. There wasn’t anyone who didn’t love him,
except perhaps the guard dog at his junkyard, which bit him on more than one
occasion.
After ending his term as Grand Master, he continued to volunteer and
remained active in his community and lodge. In the last few years of his life, his
health began to decline. Diabetes created circulation problems in his feet that
resulted in the amputations of first one foot and lower leg and then the other.
C. Ray did not let that stop him. He was excited to get two prosthetic legs and
to be able to walk again without pain. COVID restrictions prevented that from
happening. C. Ray learned to use Zoom to stay in contact with his lodge and
friends. The night he passed away, he had RSVP’d for an online Table Lodge.
On May 18, 2021, the Great Architect of the Universe called C. Ray from labor
to refreshment and welcomed him into that celestial lodge above.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

21

Most Worshipful Whitaker was a humble, helpful, God-fearing man who
was grateful for all of the blessings of life. He always had time to talk to anyone,
young and old, no matter their station in life. He was always willing to go the
extra mile to help others, and never left anyone he met in need. C. Ray lived
our Masonic ideals and was an example for all of us to emulate. He is greatly
missed by his family, his lodge brothers, and his community. He truly made a
difference in his life.
Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy resting place! Bright and glorious
be thy rising from it!

EULOGY
ALVIN J. WEIS
On July 18 of this year, Most Worshipful Brother Alvin J. Weis laid down his
working tools at the age of 86 years. I was privileged to serve as his Grand
Secretary, and came to know him well, not only during his years on the Masonic
Homes Board, but also as he progressed through the line to become Grand
Master on October 13, 1999.
Many of his friends knew him as A.J., but his beloved wife, Ginny, called
him Al, and that is the name I used during all the years that I knew him. We
traveled together through the years, and when you do that, you get to know
someone well. So this is a personal message today, with some reflections on
the man and the Mason that I knew.
Al was born in Southern California, but his family moved to Manteca, where
he attended school and where he also had his first contact with Freemasonry.
He joined Manteca Chapter, Order of DeMolay, and served it as its Master
Councilor. The principles taught in the Order of DeMolay shaped his life in
significant ways, and in our travels we often talked about DeMolay and its impact
on both our lives. He continued to support DeMolay throughout his life, serving
as a Chapter Dad and as a member of the board of directors for the Northern
California DeMolay Foundation.
He petitioned Tyrian Lodge No. 439 in Manteca in 1966, and was raised a
Master Mason on September 20 of that year. When his job with Pacific Gas and
Electric required a move to the Bay Area, he affiliated with Acalanes-Fellowship
Lodge No. 480, and served that lodge as its Master in 1981. In 1983 he was
appointed Grand Marshal by Most Worshipful Brother Arthur Haglund, and
during that year traveled widely with his Grand Master. He was then appointed
as a Trustee of the Masonic Homes of California and served on that board for
12 years.
Of all the avenues of service for our Grand Lodge that he filled, perhaps
the one closest to his heart was that of a Trustee of the Homes Board. In those
days, it was customary for individual trustees to interview children who were
recommended for our Masonic Home for Children at Covina, and he took
that assignment seriously. His compassion for those in great need gave him
the empathy and ability to do that job with skill and assiduity, and he devoted
himself to each assignment as only a dedicated Mason can.
During his tenure as Grand Master, the Masonic Grand Lodge of California
celebrated its 150th anniversary, and he proudly recounted one very important moment of the year in his Grand Master’s Message at the 151st Annual
Communication, over which he presided. On April 13 of that year, he was

24

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

received on the floor of the California State Senate, along with the Grand
Master of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Most Worshipful Brother
Ronald Robinson, and presented a commemorative certificate of the occasion
to the Senate. As far as we know, they were the only two Grand Masters ever
so honored by our legislature with this signal privilege. Al said in his message
that “the harmonious fellowship existing between our two Grand Lodges was
visible to the political leadership of the State of California, and a new era of
fraternal goodwill began.”
There are many stories that I could tell about Past Grand Master Alvin J.
Weis, but I will leave you with one that shows the depth of his commitment to
the principles of our ancient Craft.
On Wednesday, October 13, 1999, the Grand Lodge was scheduled to install
the newly elected and appointed Grand Lodge Officers at 11 a.m. As the time
approached, we looked around for Al so that we could begin on time. No Al.
Where was he? We were getting worried. Surely, he would not have forgotten that
he was to be installed as Grand Master of Masons that morning. Then, almost
at the last minute, he showed up. Where had he been? What had happened?
He told us simply that it had been his turn to mow the lawn for a widow of
his lodge, and that he needed to take care of that duty before anything else. He
had driven from San Francisco across the Bay Bridge to Lafayette, where his
lodge was located, and mowed her lawn, returning to Grand Lodge afterward.
You see, it was more important to him to do his duty as a Mason than it was
to be installed as Grand Master of Masons in California. He always had his
priorities straight. May each of us as Masons live our lives the same way that
Alvin Jesse Weis did—discharging our duties as Masons before anything else!
The Grand Organist provided a musical selection, following which the
Grand Master thanked both the Grand Organist and Most Worshipful Brother
Cooper.

Remarks from the Youth Orders

Miss Jessica Anderson
Miss California Job’s Daughters
Good morning Most Worshipful Weiss, honored guests, and visitors. My name
is Jessica Anderson, and I am Miss California Job’s Daughter 2021-22. Thank
you so much for giving me the distinct honor of speaking today on behalf of
California Job’s Daughters.
My theme for my term as the Miss California Job’s Daughter is “Exhale Fear,
Inhale Courage.” This theme goes hand in hand with your theme of “Embracing
the Next Evolution.” For many, change can be intimidating. It’s so easy to get
comfortable with your life and not embrace the chapters that are to come
next. To evolve, grow, and develop both as people and organizations, we must
embrace these changes while remaining true to ourselves and our values. In
order to embrace the next evolution, exhale your fears and inhale the courage
you need to be open to that change.
For the past 18 months, our world has been in constant motion. New adaptations are needed faster than we could have anticipated. This has not been the
case just for our personal lives, but within our Masonic family. So much change
has been thrust upon all of us, but we have gracefully embraced that change.
Although it has been almost two years full of loss and suffering, we have not
allowed our Masonic family to fade away in the process. We have not been lost
during our new evolution. Instead, we have graciously embraced it. We have
found new ways to engage our members and new ways to connect our brothers,
sisters, and families throughout our state. By embracing technologies made
possible and mainstreamed during a time of constant change, we were able to
embrace the new futures for our orders. The organizations that entered this
pandemic are not the same as those exiting it. Many of us have found a new
love for our organizations, and the fire was relit under us to pour that love and

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

35

devotion back into them. Instead of choosing to hit pause when the world shut
down, our Masonic groups continued to thrive. Our wonderful adults found a
new way to engage our youth, making sure no one felt left behind or forgotten
as our evolution took place. Our groups are stronger than ever as a result of our
drive and the anticipation of being able to see one another face-to-face again.
While celebrating our organizations’ futures, it’s also important to honor
their pasts. While moving forward, we cannot forget where we came from. As
we enter the next phase of our Masonic evolution, I feel it’s important to share
with you the parallels I see from when Job’s Daughters was founded. Job’s
Daughters was founded in 1920 by Ethel T. Wead Mick. People of her time were
embracing an evolution of their own. Job’s Daughters was founded right around
the time of the women’s suffrage movement and the end of a global pandemic.
Ethel T. Wead Mick created a place for women to learn the skills needed to
adapt to their changing world. These skills are still being taught today to Job’s
Daughters throughout the world as we, 101 years later, find ourselves working
our way out of another global pandemic.
My nine years in Job’s Daughters has impacted my life in more ways than
I can count. Job’s Daughters has given me the resources to achieve so many
milestones, many of which would not have been possible without the wonderful
and supportive adults and Masons from my lodge in Simi Valley. These Masons
and adults played a key role in me being crowned the new Miss California Job’s
Daughter this past August. As I have embarked on my journey, they continue
to support and inspire me to make them proud every day.
On the drive down the mountain into Simi Valley, there’s a smiley face
etched into the first mountain you see when you enter our city. Throughout
my life, this mountain has signified being home. For my pin and charm design, I
included a mountain with a smiley face engraved on it. This year on my travels,
I will be far from friends and family, but every time I look at my charm I will be
at home. For many, our Masonic families are our home, and I hope my charm
reminds others that no matter the physical distance, you will always have a
family within our organization.
I would like to say a thank-you to all the adults in the room this morning.
Each and every one of you has had a profound impact on the Masonic youth of
today, and your support will cause them to go far. I look forward to seeing our
organizations reach a new chapter and embrace the new evolution of change
together.
Thank you!
Brian Davis, Master Councilor
Northern California Jurisdiction, DeMolay International
Most Worshipful Weiss, Grand Lodge Line Officers, guests and friends here
assembled, good evening! My name is Brian Davis, Master Councilor of the
Northern California DeMolay Association. Joining me today is Hannah Kolden,

36

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Sweetheart of Northern California; Michael Cherry, Deputy Master Councilor
of Northern California; Annalise Kirkley, Princess of Northern California;
Seth Bonnin, Senior Councilor of Northern California; Dad David Killmer,
Jurisdictional Advisor; and Dad Terry Peters, Executive Officer of Northern
California DeMolay (and Grand Junior Councilor of DeMolay International).
From the day I received the invitation for this event, I knew exactly where
I wanted to go with this speech. You see, it was explained in the invitation that
the Grand Master’s theme was “Embracing the Next Evolution.” As soon as
I read that, I thought “Well, that’s DeMolay. That’s the next evolution, if you
ask me.” But I was stuck on how to make an entire speech around it; I didn’t
know how to say, in a different way, that which had been said before so many
times. I didn’t want to tell you the history of DeMolay, that which you’ve heard
before, and I didn’t want to ask you for more support, that which you already
give so much.
Youth leaders like myself have on many occasions stood before lodges
of Masons and presented to them the reasons they should sponsor a chapter.
Many have stood at events like this and explained the subtle ways Masons can
support the youth, through mentorship or through allowing a chapter to meet
at their lodge. This has all been said before, in every iteration you can imagine.
Instead, I wanted to focus on two very important words: thank you.
From the beginning, in 1919, when Dad Land founded the Mother Chapter
in Kansas City, the Masons have provided support to the young men of this
country, and around the world, recognizing then that they were the next evolution. Dad Land started the chapter with nine young men who were in need
of guidance, who were in need of a figure to help them live upright, courteous,
compassionate lives, for they no longer had such figures in their lives. Every
year, DeMolays make trips to visit Dad Land’s grave to speak to him, again and
again, those important two words: thank You
Did you know that the first man to walk on the moon was a DeMolay?
That’s a genuine question, because until about a month ago, I certainly did
not, and I am a huge nerd when it comes to space (it’s true; it’s a big interest of
mine). The first man to step on the moon was a DeMolay. The Second Man to
step on the moon was a Mason and a Dad Advisor. This means that a DeMolay
and a Mason were among the first to touch the stars. You always hear advisers
say “shoot for the moon,” but how many of them think you’ll take it literally?
Neil Armstrong clearly did. He is already one of the most inspiring figures of
the past century, but to DeMolays (all the ones I’ve told, at least), it creates an
even bigger impact. That man was once someone just like you: he did the same
Ritual, held the same positions, and I’ll bet he even influenced his community,
as a DeMolay, in much the same way you and your chapter do today. Let us not
forget Buzz Aldrin, a Mason, standing side by side with a DeMolay on the most
harrowing and incredible feat of human engineering and ingenuity—in history?
Can we say in all of history?
To you, Brother Armstrong, and to you, Dad Aldrin, we say: thank you

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

37

Those words, “thank you,” are what I wanted to emphasize above all today.
Those two words go a long way to showing the appreciation we have for the
hard work all of you here have done for us, the DeMolays. It goes a long way to
showing our gratitude toward those two men who touched the stars 52 years
ago, who inspired an entire generation of scientists and dreamers who wished,
like them, to push deeper into the final frontier. Those two words go a long
way towards showing our infinite appreciation to Dad Land, who did what he
could to advice and counsel those nine young men more than 100 years ago, and
unknowingly paved the way for thousands of young men around the world to
come together with Masons, like yourself, to receive guidance and push them,
too, to touch the stars.
You are a part of that long history now. You all, in this room, have the
potential to change the life of a young man like me. Many of you already have,
and some of you have without even realizing it. It doesn’t take much. Perhaps
it’s as simple as offering a warm welcome when they visit the lodge, to show
that life isn’t always cold and unloving; or as complex as encouraging a young
man to pursue his interest in starting a business, and guiding him along the
way on the mistakes you made so he doesn’t make the same ones. You can
embrace the next evolution and guide us to touch the stars once again. And for
this work, for your efforts, and for your support now, in the past, and far into
the future, I say: thank you.
Because it can’t be stated enough, I would like now to express my personal
gratitude toward you, Dad Weiss, for your continuing and unceasing support.
Members of this Grand Lodge and the Masons in the room have impacted my
life greatly, and helped me to better myself before my peers. Truly, thank you
all for supporting me in my nine years as a DeMolay.
Lastly, I would like to invite you all to our Annual Convention, taking place
just a short distance from here at the Hyatt Regency in Burlingame November
26-28. You can register online on our website norcaldemolay.com.
I wish to make it my goal through the end of the year to ask each member
to thank a masonic adviser in their life, knowing that it is you who help us to
do good work and be better men. Thank you.
Miss Katie Sullivan, Grand Worthy Advisor
International Order of Rainbow
Most Worshipful Grand Master Weiss, officers and members of Grand Lodge,
distinguished and honored guests, and friends of California Rainbow, hello! I am

At Southern California Jurisdictions Conclave, Worshipful Grand Master
Weiss spoke about the Grand Lodge’s strategic plan of 2050. He spoke of the
future of our Masonic bodies, and it made me think of where I will be in 2050.
It also reminded me of stories I’d heard about from 30 years ago. Several stories

38

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

involved three members who were from different towns and different DeMolay
chapters, yet they became close friends. They would talk on the phone late at
night, planning their next DeMolay adventure, and then there would be repercussions for something called long-distance phone calls? If anyone can explain
that to me, that would be great. They would spend their days making something
called a cassette tape so they could listen to music in the car on their way to
dances with Rainbow Girls and Job’s Daughters. I have heard of cassette tapes,
but again, if someone could explain this to me, I would greatly appreciate it. I
think the stories that seemed the most fun were ones about their great adviser,
who took them throughout Northern California. They would spend weekends
visiting other divisions, writing newsletters, and just having a great time. He
must have been an amazing adviser, because not only did he create unforgettable experiences, but he taught them about leadership, brotherhood, and the
lessons of Masonry.
I wonder if that Mason knew the impact he was having? For those of us who
have had the privilege of being part of one of our great Masonic youth organizations, I encourage you to think of that one adult who encouraged the value of
brotherhood or sisterhood, who demonstrated to you how to be a leader, and
who shared the lessons of our Masonic orders. Did he or she know their impact
would continue? Remember those three DeMolay boys I mentioned earlier? They
were leaders then, and they are leaders now. One adviser can make a difference.
The three DeMolays I mentioned serve in leadership roles in the Masonic
family today. Jim Sullivan, my dad, is a member of California Rainbow’s Grand
Executive Committee. Uncle James—but you may know him as Dad James
Banta—is Northern California DeMolay’s Executive Director. And the third your
very own Worshipful Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California Allen
Casalou. They continue to share their experiences as DeMolay, which shows
how close they were then and still are today. The question is, would they still
be here if that adviser hadn’t invested in them? Would you still be here today
if the adviser you thought of earlier hadn’t invested in you? Through the acts
of encouraging you, laughing with you, and working with you toward the goals
you wanted to accomplish, they had an impact.
A youth adviser who embodies the tenets of our Masonic family has an
impact that can last a lifetime. Remember the adviser I asked you to think of?
How would your organization look if they had not made, and continued to
make, the investments they have. Their legacy continues to support our orders
today. Please stand if you are active in supporting a youth order. We thank you
for your support in inspiring us to grow.
We all need that one adult, because that one person can and will make a
difference in our Masonic family. If it were not for the unconditional support
and investment of my adviser, I would not be standing here today. The countless
hours she spent working with me at her kitchen table reviewing my memory
work, the unforgettable Rainbow road trips, where U-turns were always a
necessity, and her continuous investment in my future will forever remain in

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

my heart. I hope to someday be able to create that same environment of endless

I leave you with this challenge to make a difference right now as an adult.
We aren’t born leaders; we learn from those before us. Your investment of

For a full year, our jurisdiction was in an unprecedented situation. We faced

our theme this year is “Sailing to New Shores.” Our first objective is to get new
members and chapters on board. To help them navigate, we will be modernizing
how we approach communication, membership, and our relations with other
Masonic bodies. We will hold true to our traditions, but modern problems do
require modern solutions. It is especially appropriate that we focus on the future
of our organization, because the members of today are the leaders of tomorrow.
But our chapters cannot sail alone. We need strong adult leaders to help
us navigate uncharted waters, to steer us back on course when the winds don’t
go our way. So I would encourage you all to reach out to your local chapters
and see how you can help them. Become an adviser, give the local chapters and
leagues the opportunity to use your lodges, and help out with events if you can.
If you have sons, grandsons, or nephews who are of age, invite them to an event
at your local chapter.

Grand Master’s Youth Support Award
The Grand Master announced that four brothers had been selected to receive
the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award to recognize their outstanding contribution to the Masonic youth orders. The Grand Master then called upon
Worshipful Jeffrey M. Schimsky, a Past Master of Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674 and
Vice Chairman of the Grand Lodge Youth Orders Committee, to assist him in
presenting the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award to the following honorees.
Matthew E. Arnold
Matthew E. Arnold’s role in the U.S. Navy has taken him and his family around
the world. In turn, they’ve brought with them a deep devotion to the Masonic
youth orders, no matter where they find themselves.
A Navy captain and father of five, Brother Arnold has been surrounded by
the youth orders since childhood, when he served as a master councilor for
Ohio DeMolay. Since moving to San Diego, where he affiliated with Consuelo
Lodge No. 325 in 1993 (later San Diego No. 35), he’s continued that association,
serving first as Associate Bethel Guardian for Job’s Daughters California.
His own children have been affiliated with Job’s Daughters, Rainbow for
Girls, and the Order of DeMolay; Brother Arnold’s wife, Melissa, is also a Past
Honored Queen of Job’s Daughters. In addition to his work with Job’s Daughters,
Brother Arnold has been an active member of the Rainbow for Girls advisory
board and served as the advisory council chairman for the San Diego chapter of
DeMolay. Given his constant moving, it’s no surprise that the family has been
active in Job’s Daughters around the world, including in Virginia and Australia,
where his daughter retains a dual membership in Bethel No. 24 of Moreton Bay,
Queensland.
As a passionate advocate for the youth orders, Brother Arnold has displayed
the qualities that make a committed adult leader, and his contributions have
been felt deeply by those around him.
Patrick D. Quinn
The COVID-19 pandemic took a severe toll on membership organizations of
all kinds. Luckily for the members of the Castro Valley chapter of the Order
of DeMolay, Patrick Quinn has shown what it takes to keep the organization
going strong.
Brother Quinn first joined DeMolay in 1977 as a member of the Hayward
area chapter. After being raised a Master Mason with Crow Canyon No. 551 in

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

41

2010, he returned to DeMolay to become an adult adviser. Faced at the time with
declining participation, Quinn assumed the role of chapter adviser in Castro
Valley to help keep the unit afloat. In 2017, he took on the role of chairman of
the advisory council and, despite having no other advisers around him, managed
to attract and recruit new adult leaders to serve the chapter and new youth
members to rebuild the organization and help it grow.
Throughout the pandemic, the Castro Valley chapter has remained active
and engaged, a testament to Brother Quinn’s efforts. In recognition of his
service, Brother Quinn was presented the degree of Chevalier and the Cross
of Honor. In addition to his work with the youth orders, Quinn serves as lodge
treasurer for Crow Canyon No. 551, is involved with the Aahmes Shrine, and
in 2019 was presented with the Hiram Award for service to his lodge. Outside
Masonry, he serves on the executive board of the International Brotherhood
of Electrical Workers Local No. 595 in Pleasanton, where he lives with his wife,
Donna Jo.
Jeffrey W. Askins
For most, Freemasonry provides one’s first exposure to the youth orders. For
Jeff Askins, it was the other way around—and both California Rainbow and
California Masonry are better off for it.
Since 1999, when his daughter joined the International Order of Rainbow
for Girls, Worshipful Brother Askins has become an integral part of both organizations. He’s served Rainbow as an advisory board member, been selected as
the assembly Rainbow Dad, and been a member of the Grand Assembly floor
crew. In 2013, he was appointed as state Rainbow Dad, and the following year to
serve on the grand executive committee. A tireless behind-the-scenes worker,
he’s helped ensure that Grand Assembly comes off without a hitch each year, and
along with his wife, Laura, has chaired the Northern Camp for nearly a decade,
providing countless members with an ability to experience the outdoors. In
recognition of his service to Rainbow, he was given the Grand Cross of Color,
the organization’s highest award.
Worshipful Brother Askins has brought the same dedication to Freemasonry.
In 2002, he petitioned Rio Linda Lodge No. 786 and was raised a Master Mason
in 2007, serving as lodge master in 2011. He has also served as an officer coach
for Oak Plains No. 789, where he affiliated in 2016. That same year, he was
presented the Hiram Award for service to Rio Linda No. 786.
Ralph C. Shelton II
There are few jobs or titles that Ralph Shelton hasn't held for the Order of
DeMolay. He’s served the organization at the chapter, league, and jurisdiction
levels, and it’s not unusual for him to hold multiple positions at a time. At

42

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

present, he serves as a member of two chapter advisory boards (Lake Forest
and Orange), is an administrador for the league, and is director of membership
for Southern California DeMolay.
His record of accomplishments is indeed vast: He has earned the Cross of
Honor and the Legion of Honor, has served as dean of the Southern California
Legion of Honor Preceptory, and is a deputy member of the International
Supreme Council for the Order of DeMolay. However, Worshipful Brother
Shelton has never been one to seek out titles or honors. Rather, they’re a testament to a lifetime in DeMolay—of having spent the past 40 years as an active
member and adult leader.
Much of the work that Worshipful Brother Shelton, a longtime member
of several Masonic lodges and Past Master of Orange Grove No. 293, puts into
DeMolay is done out of sight—but is crucial to the operation of the organization.
In all, he sets a tremendous example of hard work and dedication to the youth
he serves, and in so doing, prepares today’s youth members to grow into the
adult leaders of tomorrow.
Grand Master’s Mason of the Year Award
The Grand Master announced that two brothers had been selected to receive
the Grand Master’s Mason of the Year Award to recognize their outstanding
dedication and service. The Grand Master then called upon the Grand Secretary
to assist him in presenting the Grand Master’s Mason of the Year Award to the
following honorees.
Robert L. Boyce
The ideals of Masonry aren’t meant to exist only inside the lodge room. Few
Masons better exemplify that than Robert Boyce.
Quietly and without fanfare, Brother Boyce has made it his mission to be
of service not only to his lodge, but to his community. During the COVID-19
shutdown, he delivered much-needed food and essentials to elderly members
and Masonic widows throughout his region, and during the holidays he and
his wife, Teresa, cooked and delivered special dinners to the needy. He has
continued to keep in regular contact with elderly members and widows since
then, helping deliver groceries and other supplies and instituting a ride-sharing
program to ensure Masons and widows were able to receive their COVID-19
vaccination shots.
Worshipful Brother Boyce was raised in Nevada Lodge No. 13 in 2007, and
in 2013 he affiliated with Corinthian-Hammonton Lodge No. 9 in Marysville.
In 2017 he served as lodge master and since 2018 has been a district inspector.
He is also a member of the Ben Ali Shrine, where he is president of the Central
Sacramento Valley Shrine Club. However, it’s his work with the Masonic youth
orders that has endeared him to so many. He was instrumental in reestablishing

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

43

the Liberty Chapter of DeMolay and Bethel No. 256 of Job’s Daughters in Yuba
City, and he continues to work with both groups closely.
Brother Boyce’s service to Freemasonry and to his fellow members and
their families is in keeping with the highest traditions of the Fraternity and sets
an example for all to follow.
Robert E. Bronner
As a licensed pyrotechnic engineer, Robert Bronner is used to creating the
spectacular. And yet it’s not that flashy and awe-inspiring work that has made
him such an important figure to his lodge; rather, it’s his persistence and dayto-day reliability.
Brother Bronner is described as the go-to man for getting new lodge projects off the ground at Fontana No. 653. A three-term lodge master (2015, 2016,
2019), he has helped bring several programs and efforts to life at Fontana Lodge.
Chief among those was establishing a vendor booth for Raising A Reader, the
California Masonic Foundation literacy partner, at several comic-book conventions throughout Southern California. Those booths, which helped raise
awareness of the literacy nonprofit and brought it to new school districts,
were staffed by members of the Masonic youth orders, allowing those students
to gain valuable experience and be of service to their communities. He also
helps coordinate the annual Poinsettia Ball, bringing Masons and their spouses
together in support of Masonic charities. And while serving as lodge master,
he coauthored a bill to allow qualified Master Masons to share in the delivery
of full-form lectures for the Entered Apprentice and Master Mason degrees,
thereby increasing lodge participation in the Ritual work.
With his can-do attitude and willingness to serve, Brother Bronner is an
inspiration to his lodge and to Masons everywhere.

GRAND MASTER’S ANNUAL MESSAGE
October 8, 2021

Visiting Dignitaries and honored guests, our Grand Lodge Officers, our
Past Grand Masters, members of the Grand Lodge, and brethren all,
I am pleased to stand before you today to report that your Grand Lodge
and the Masons of California have emerged from the long shadow cast by this
pandemic. One year ago, I stood before you and laid out our bold new path forward to a brighter future. Today it is my pleasure to report that we have made
amazing progress embracing our next evolution and are positioned to continue
moving upward and outward toward our ultimate goal, a world in harmony.
When this year began, we still faced an uncertain future, with an unknowable timeline for the resumption of our activities. While I was eager to get
started on my strategic priorities for this year, one new priority superseded all
others in its urgency: reopening the Fraternity. Thanks to the brethren’s passage of Most Worshipful Trauner’s Recommendation No. 1 at our 171st Annual
Communication, I took the first step immediately by issuing a directive allowing virtual Stated Meetings per a script prepared and approved by our Ritual
Committee. This allowed the brethren to conduct official business meetings,
elections, and Installations while still unable to meet in person.
Every change carries with it both good and poor aspects. Moving to Zoom
deprived us for several months of the opportunity to share refreshment and
reduced the quality of our fellowship. But at the same time, the use of technology allowed those who might not otherwise have been able to participate
the opportunity to join us. At my Installation last year, over 40 percent more
people joined the video streaming than the number we would have expected to
attend in person. I was able to get to far more Lodge Installations than I would
have been able to attend had I needed to travel to each one, and many of those
Lodge Installations also had increased attendance than in years past. And as
we saw this trend, through the use of technology, it became apparent that we
would have to find a way to retain as many of these benefits as possible when
we re-opened. But these benefits could not fully make up for our need to be
together and did not lessen the urgency of our reopening priority.
For this reason, as vaccines were authorized for distribution, your Grand
Lodge began discussions with the California Department of Health about defining specific criteria aimed at fraternal and service organizations such as ours. In
April, the state created the Private Events category, whose guidelines allowed

50

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

me to issue a directive authorizing in-person Stated Meetings within certain
constraints. Many of our lodges took advantage of this opportunity to begin
meeting in person.
In late May, the governor announced he would remove his statewide restrictions effective June 15. I subsequently issued a further directive on June 1 removing all meeting restrictions other than those imposed by any local mandates,
allowing lodges to choose, at the Master’s discretion, whether to restart in-person meetings or continue remotely. Our lodges have since reopened, degree
work has resumed, and our many in-person events are being held once again.
But as our Masonic year turns and my directives terminate, we must not
forget what we have learned from this experience. We must use this hard-won
knowledge to the benefit of the Fraternity. If the pandemic taught us anything,
it’s that communication technology has reached such a level of maturity that
using it to enhance the Masonic meeting experience must become commonplace. It allowed us to conduct business when we were unable to be together
in person. It allowed participation by remotely located brethren. It opened
up whole new Masonic education possibilities by enabling brethren to learn
directly from the world’s Masonic scholars, wherever they might be. It also
allowed interested prospects to gain quicker insights into the fraternity, and
helped them make that life-changing decision to join us. We must integrate
this technology permanently as our Fraternity moves forward. I will shortly be
placing a recommendation before you to take this next step.
While the pandemic has impacted much of what we do, it has not swayed us
from pursuing our future. Undeterred by the challenges, the Fraternity moved
forward this past year with the objectives of our 2025 Fraternity Plan as part of
our 30-year vision for Masonry in California, “The World in Harmony,” which
we aspire to achieve by 2050, the bicentennial year of our Grand Lodge.
As was rolled out in full last April, the 2025 Plan embodies three strategic
goals, or pillars, by which our actions should be guided at the lodge and the
Grand Lodge level. Pillar One, True Friendship, is our cornerstone. The deep
relationships and level of trust between brethren is the unique hallmark of our
Fraternity. We must teach our brethren, as well as our communities, what true
friendship can really mean. To do this, our lodges must be efficient, nimble,
and well managed.
One area of the lodge experience where the brethren have expressed a desire
for meaningful improvement is the planning and conduct of Stated Meetings
and other events and activities. Our data from last year showed us that those
lodges which have an executive committee process are better organized, more
transparent, and more effective in their interactions with their members. They
are also better able to provide consistency in planning and efficiency in their
management. One of the key strengths of our Grand Lodge is our Executive
Committee. Not only does it provide the opportunity to approach issues from
a variety of viewpoints in a safe and cooperative environment, but it also provides consistency of direction across multiple years. Each decision, made by

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

51

the Executive Committee as a whole, has enough time for full implementation
rather than being limited to just one year. As we work toward our 2050 vision,
I believe every lodge should be using the Executive Committee model. Shortly,
I will propose a recommendation to establish the Executive Committee as a
standing committee of every lodge.
But the Executive Committee model still requires that each individual
leader, coming into the committee, be as prepared as possible to make their best
contribution to the group. To this end, three years ago, under Most Worshipful
Stuart Wright, Grand Lodge formed a Special Committee on Leadership
Development to conduct a thorough reassessment of our Fraternity leadership-training practices and to recommend changes going forward to optimize the
program. We set a three-year horizon for this work, and I am pleased to report
that the committee has exceeded our expectations. We now have a full set of
recommendations, for review and implementation in the coming year, for programs aimed at developing members from prospect to Master Mason, training
Lodge and Hall Association leadership, refreshing the Inspector Development
curriculum, and training AGLs, Constitutional Board members, and committee members. My sincerest gratitude goes to the steering committee—Right
Worshipful Sean Metroka, Mark Nielsen, David Rathgeber, Very Worshipful Jack
Rose, Jordan Yelinek, and Most Worshipful David Doan—to the subcommittee
chairman, and to all the committee members for their outstanding effort to
complete this major undertaking.
True Friendship must also extend beyond our own Jurisdiction. To this end,
our Grand Lodge continues to play a leading role in the Western Conference of
Grand Lodges. Two years ago, we began working with our Executive Committee
counterparts to increase communication and better integrate Masonry across all
the western jurisdictions. Together we initiated a semiannual virtual meeting,
separate from the Conference of Grand Masters of North America, to better
address ongoing issues of mutual interest and increase the effectiveness of the
conference. As a result, this year our Grand Lodge was requested to host and
lead the next conference in February 2022, in Milwaukee. We look forward to
working more closely with our neighboring Grand Lodges to share useful ideas
and experiences.
At the local level, our new lodge development efforts continued to bear
fruit. This year we instituted four new lodges, and several others are being
contemplated. Eight lodges currently under dispensation have petitioned for
their charters at this Annual Communication. It is exciting to see these incipient
lodges and the enthusiasm their members bring to the Craft.
Unfortunately, at the other end of the spectrum, we also have a few lodges
who have not been able to work together in harmony. At the start of this year,
I continued the suspension of Artesia Sunrise Lodge No. 377 and Van Nuys
Lodge No. 450. Artesia Sunrise has diligently worked to correct their issues,
and I was pleased to reinstate their charter this year. Van Nuys Lodge has made
little progress over the past two years toward rectifying their many issues. After

52

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

a thorough review by the Inspector, AGL, Grand Lodge staff, and the Executive
Committee, it is apparent that this lodge will not be able to address the numerous issues causing its suspension. Based on this conclusion, at the proper time
during this Annual Communication, I will be recommending that the charter
of this lodge be revoked.
Some audit irregularities found this year required the suspension of
International Cities Lodge No. 389. They are currently working to correct the
issues found, and I have no doubt they will soon meet the requirements to
have their charter reinstated. Riverside Lodge No. 635 was also suspended for a
number of financial management and leadership issues. After much discussion,
the lodge has voted to surrender their charter.
I am very excited with the progress that we have made on our True
Friendship Pillar this year. I look forward to seeing the implementation of our
new training programs and the anticipated growth in numbers, members, and
stability in our lodges.
Pillar Two of our plan, Diversity and Harmony, will help us better practice
the values we espouse: tolerance for diverse opinions, religions, and backgrounds, especially at all levels of leadership. There is much the entire Masonic
family can do, working together, to bring people of different cultures, traditions,
and perspectives together. Doing so will set a standard and serve as a model for
our communities to embrace as we work to move forward to a world in harmony.
But accomplishing this vision will require support, not just from our lodges,
but from the entire Masonic family. Every Masonic body, our chapters, our
valleys, our courts, our Shrine temples—all of our affiliated bodies will need to
play their role to achieve a world in harmony. I believe that our organizational
structure tends to silo our various branches, and integrated activity and communication across our bodies has declined. As a first step to addressing this
issue, I asked every division to host a Masonic family unity event this year to
bring the entire family of Freemasonry together, to reacquaint ourselves with
each other, and to begin the transition away from the pandemic. These events
were incredibly successful! Attendance averaged nearly 200, our youth leaders
talked about each of their orders, we ate excellent food, and in some instances
we even had entertainment. I thank all of the AGLs, Inspectors, Masters, and
lodges who worked diligently to make each event a true success. I hope that
moving forward, our lodges and Grand Lodge will look for more opportunities
to build these bridges and break down these silos so that we bond more closely
with those whom we already know share our values and advance our purpose.
Full support of our youth orders is also essential to Masonic family unity.
This year, I was able to send virtual greetings to Grand Bethel, virtually attend
Grand Assembly and the NorCal DeMolay Convention, and attend SoCal
DeMolay Conclave in person. All of these sessions were creatively executed in
spite of the pandemic constraints. Just think, the young adults who now lead
our youth orders will be the leaders of our Fraternity in our bicentennial year.
It is exciting to think that I may have met and talked with the future Grand

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

53

Master, or the SGIG, the Worthy Grand Matron, or the Supreme Royal Matron
of 2050. I know that our fraternity will be in good hands under the leadership
of these exceptional young men and women. I thank Most Worshipful Russ
Charvonia for his outstanding advocacy and leadership of our Youth Orders
Committee and program.
For over 25 years, our Grand Lodge has enjoyed a fraternal relationship with
the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California. I firmly believe that
it is now time to discuss how we can build on this mutual experience and evolve
our relationship to the next level. We have begun discussions with the Prince
Hall Grand Lodge leadership, and I am pleased to report that Most Worshipful
David San Juan agrees that now is the moment. Last year, we created a Special
Committee on Fraternal Relations, led by MW David Doan, and now MW San
Juan is moving to do the same. It is my hope that over the next year, the committees will meet together to explore the many opportunities we have to grow
an even stronger relationship than that which exists today.
And to involve all the recognized Grand Lodges sharing our geographic
jurisdiction in plotting a course beneficial to Masonry, I asked MW George
Issaians, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile, to meet with MW
David San Juan and myself. Both agreed enthusiastically, and we held our first
discussion of shared goals, hopes, and dreams for Freemasonry in California in
September. I look forward to this dialogue continuing between our leaderships
in the months to come.
To bring the world to harmony, we must live the change we want to see
in the world. By encouraging our ties to our Masonic family bodies, our youth
orders and our fellow California Grand Lodges, we raise our ability to work
together to foster and promote the Masonic values of tolerance, diversity, and
inclusion. But for these values to improve our communities and bring the world
into harmony, what we do must be known and recognized in those communities.
Pillar Three, Positive Awareness, addresses our image and branding with
the public. For too long we have allowed others to write our narrative, often
based on exaggerated and false images. To correct these misperceptions, often
fostered by those with an anti-Masonic agenda, we must take the initiative and
educate the public on who we are, what we stand for and what we do to benefit
our communities and the world at large. Bonding with our fellow Grand Lodges,
affiliated Bodies and Youth Groups gives us the ability to show Masonry in a way
that lets every member of the public see someone in the Masonic Family that
looks just like them, so that they can connect with the values we espouse and
appreciate our good works. In the next quarter, we will roll out the most aggressive public relations campaign we have ever attempted, to advance this goal.
Our benefits to society are most easily illustrated through our philanthropy.
To continue growing our ability to help others, we must keep our philanthropic
arms strong. As part of periodically reassessing our Grand Lodge organizational
structure, we recognized that as our fund-raising expectations increased, the
central point for all fund raising should be the California Masonic Foundation.

54

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

But to do this successfully required a structural change in our governing policies
for our Board of Trustees. In 2019, we began a process to move the organizational
chart and reporting functions of the Foundation staff to the Board of Trustees,
to structure the Foundation in a manner similar to that used successfully by
the Masonic Homes of California and Acacia Creek. That re-alignment was
completed on April 1 of this year. This gives the Board increased flexibility and
capability to assure that the fund-raising goals of both the Masonic Homes of
California and the Foundation’s programs are successfully met. And the first
efforts under this new structure have produced exemplary results.
The Foundation’s performance has produced the best year yet for annual
giving from our brethren. In addition to record levels of donations to the Annual
Fund, the continuance of our Distressed Worthy Brother Fund, and a fantastic
year for Masons 4 Mitts, the Foundation kicked off our new planned giving
campaign based on our Cornerstone Society. Planned gifts are the most important way we maintain the Masonic Homes of California and our Foundation’s
programs. I hope all members will consider leaving a bequest in their estate
plans. I thank Most Worshipful John Heisner and CEO Doug Ismail for their
creative leadership of the Foundation.
In addition to the growing impact of our Masonic Outreach Services, the
innovative health care approaches pioneered by our Masonic Center for Youth
and Families are increasingly successful and increasingly in demand. Our communities are in need of state-of-the-art health care for a growing number of
youth suffering from mental health issues. To address this growing need, the
Masonic Homes of California conducted a third-party study on the potential
for expanding the reach of the MCYAF. The study was completed, the recommendations have been assessed, and the Masonic Homes is poised to begin
implementing actions to achieve this goal over the next several years. I thank
MW Larry Adamson, CEO Gary Charland, and Executive Director Kimberly
Rich for their leadership and vision in working to bring this unique health care
capability to more of our brethren and our communities.
The combination of our increased efforts at philanthropy in our communities and our efforts to publicize that philanthropy should position us in the
years to come to benefit our communities and share our values, allowing us to
attract men of good character to our lodges, and to grow our ability to reach
our 2050 goal of “The World in Harmony.”
At a more personal level, our re-opening allowed me to enjoy some of the
many privileges of serving as Grand Master this year. One of the honors that a
Grand Master enjoys is presenting the Diamond Jubilee Award to those brethren achieving 75 years of membership. This year I was able to make four such
presentations. Being able to hear their stories and share in the moment with
their families was a most memorable experience. I will cherish their first-hand
accounts of some of the key moments of our history forever.
In addition, I had the honor to exercise a power embodied in the office of
the Grand Master for only the second time in this century, making a Mason at

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

55

Sight. Brother Michael Harry Will, a member of Oak Plains Lodge No. 789, was
a Fellow Craft about to be raised a Master Mason when the pandemic shutdown
began. Subsequently, he became terminally ill and was placed in hospice care.
Our brother desperately wanted to be a Master Mason, and his lodge requested
my assistance. On July 25, I made Brother Will a Master Mason at Sight. It was
one of the most heartwarming, although bittersweet, moments of the year.
Brethren, this has been a most challenging year. And yet we have accomplished almost everything I set out to achieve. This is in no small measure due to
our incredible Grand Lodge staff, beginning with our Grand Secretary. His skill
and commitment to managing our Grand Lodge operations is second to none.
Our fantastic Liberty Tour to Philadelphia would not have happened without his
direct supervision. Thank you, Very Worshipful, for your support, your insights,
and your willingness to make things happen. And thank you to each and every
member of the staff who made this journey so amazing for Barbara and me.
To the inspectors and constitutional board and committee members, thank
you for your tireless efforts on behalf of this Grand Lodge. This jurisdiction continues to be successful thanks to your dedicated service. We have two chairmen
stepping down this year: Most Worshipful Bill Bray, Chairman of our California
Masonic Memorial Temple, and Most Worshipful John Heisner, Chairman of
our California Foundation. Most Worshipfuls, thank you for your leadership
and commitment to the success of both boards. You have assured that they are
well positioned to fulfill their critical roles in the future of our Grand Lodge.
We wish you both, as well as Margo and Linda, all the best in the years ahead.
We have one Assistant Grand Lecturer retiring this year, Worshipful Al
Moen, AGL of Division VII. Thank you, Worshipful, for all the hard work and
time you have devoted to our Grand Lodge and the brethren of your lodges
these past several years. Best wishes as you and Lori begin another chapter in
your lives.
Grand Lodge Officers, thank you for your committed service under very
trying circumstances. We lost our Grand Bible Bearer, Worshipful Frank Young,
and he will always be a part of us. Thank you Worshipful Bagdasarian for your
willingness to step in and complete his term. I hope you all will remember this
year the things we accomplished, the memories we made, and the fun that we
had. I suspect our family reunions in the future will be even more enjoyable as
we make up for the time we lost. Barb and I love you all.
I also thank Sister Sarahann Shapiro, Past Grand Matron, Order of the
Eastern Star, for her five years of service as my personal secretary. Her many
ideas helped shape my thoughts and plans for this year. I truly appreciated her
ongoing support.
I could not have taken this journey without the love and support of my wife,
Barbara. I thank her for being at my side and helping to make the experience
as rewarding as it has been.
Brethren, it has been an honor to serve as your Grand Master. I feel blessed to
have been given this opportunity to serve at a difficult moment in our history. We

56

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

have weathered the pandemic and have emerged strong and ready to forge ahead.
We have embraced the next evolution of Freemasonry in California. We have a
vision we have set out to achieve. We have defined a path that will take us there.
Now we must join together as a Masonic family to make the journey successful.
Brethren, I ask you today to embrace your part in this evolution, to strive
to become the perfect ashlar. Only then will you understand the true meaning
of the cement of Brotherly Love, that cement which unites our ashlars together
to benefit the edifice they support—our society and our nation. It is the cement
of interrelationships that creates a world in harmony. Become the trowel that
spreads that cement and integrates our communities together. Our society
needs the cornerstone of Freemasonry now more than ever before. Do all you
can to make our vision a success! If we all persevere together, fortune will favor
us, and the whole world will benefit! May the Supreme Grand Master of the
Multiverse aid us in our labors. May He bless this great nation, forever watch
over our beloved Fraternity, and bring you comfort and peace, my brethren,
all the days of your lives.

Arthur H. Weiss, Grand Master
