REPORT OF THE
DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
2021–22 GRAND LODGE BUDGET

At the last Annual Communication, the brethren representing our lodges
adopted the per capita proposal I submitted as Senior Grand Warden. While so
much has changed over the past year, I am pleased to submit this budget proposal for the next Grand Lodge year, covering the period of November 1, 2021
to October 31, 2022, which will allow us to continue our important programs
and services and address our 2025 strategic plan priorities.
The COVID-19 pandemic continues to impact the finances of the Grand
Lodge. The primary impact has been with the Nob Hill Masonic Center (NHMC)
dividend earned from the parking operations at our California Masonic Memorial
Temple. Parking revenue in 2021 is forecasted to be 30 percent lower than in
2019, before the pandemic, although an improvement over the outlook at the
beginning of the pandemic in 2020.
The NHMC board of directors and executive vice president have worked
diligently to respond to the impact and create a recovery plan. The recovery
will be over an extended period, as 2021 is expected to run a modest surplus. In
2022 we are expecting a larger surplus of $162,000, but still significantly lower
than pre-pandemic levels. The reopening of San Francisco businesses and the
likelihood of large concerts and events beginning in October of this year will
allow the recovery to continue into 2022 and beyond.
Membership has also been impacted by COVID-19. Our lodges have not been
able to initiate, affiliate, or restore members other than through the Restoration
Program of the past membership year ending June 30, 2021. With the reopening
of lodges, we are planning on lodge activity getting closer to normal in 2022.
Fortunately, our Grand Lodge and related entities have been prudent in
planning for times like these. NHMC has built up operating reserves over the
years, having had to cope with the 2002 and 2008 recessions. Past Grand Master
Trauner managed the Grand Lodge finances in 2020 to accumulate a surplus.
Grand Master Weiss has done the same this year. Together these reserves will
offset the losses resulting from COVID-19 over the next several years.
The approval of this budget, which utilizes $290,000 of funds from the

68

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

operating reserve, will allow grand lodge to maintain programs and services
without creating an additional burden on per capita. The greatest need will be
in FY23 (estimated at $295,000) and lesser amounts needed in FY24 ($200,000)
and FY25 ($100,000), at which point the reserve should be mostly exhausted.
The important programs and services that will continue include:
• Financial services to lodges and halls including accounting services,
dues collection, tax return services, and tax-exempt status restoration.
The cost of Intacct is included in the budget, so lodges will only pay an
additional amount for payroll services. Halls will continue to pay fees.
• Lodge development efforts that have already resulted in the creation of
more than 30 new lodges in the state
• Leadership training events including the Master and Warden Retreats,
Secretary and Treasurer Retreats, Inspector Retreats, the Inspector
Development Academy, the Lodge Management Certification Program,
and the new Speakers Series.
• Masonic education including support for events like the International
Conference on Freemasonry and the Candidate Learning Center
• Membership management is greatly enhanced by iMember 2.0 including dues processing, now handled by Grand Lodge for those lodges
who opt into the program.
• Ritual education and training including ritual conferences for
inspectors, officer coaches, and lodge officers, and the annual ritual
competition
• Communications to Masons, widows, and the general public with the
lodge app; new lodge website templates; the California Freemason
magazine; the monthly electronic newsletter, the Leader, sent to all
lodge officers; all-member emails; social media; and the maintenance
of over 125 lodge websites. California Freemason magazine includes four
quarterly issues and the annual report.
This budget also addresses the 2025 Fraternity Plan goal of creating positive
awareness so that our members are better able to speak about Freemasonry to
their family, friends, and colleagues, and our Grand Lodge can boost our public
relations efforts across the state and increase community engagement, new
lodge and membership development.
I appreciate the great work that has been done by our Grand Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, the finance staff, and our finance committee in assisting me in
the development of this budget. I also want to thank the masters and wardens
and other attendees at our summer leadership program who provided good
feedback to me about this budget.
Brethren, I appreciate the support you gave in the adoption of the per

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

69

capita proposal last year. Our 2025 Plan lays forth the prospect of a great future
for our fraternity. I ask you to join me now in adopting this budget as we craft
leadership in our lodges and throughout our state!
Sincerely and fraternally,
Jeffery M. Wilkins, Deputy Grand Master

INSTALLATION SPEECH

Jeffery M. Wilkins, Grand Master 2021–22
Grand Lodge of California

Most Worshipful sirs, my brothers and sisters, family and guests,
I would like to start by thanking the Great Architect of the Universe for
this day and for the manifold blessings that have been bestowed upon me as I
humbly assume the position of Grand Master of Masons in California. It is hard
for me to believe that I started my Masonic journey as a simple Kansas Mason
and now I’m standing here, on this occasion, speaking to you as we start this
new Masonic year.
I would like to thank Most Worshipful Ken Nagel for nominating me and
Most Worshipful Larry Adamson, Most Worshipful John Cooper, and Most
Worshipful Steve Doan for being my installing officers today. You are a special
part of my Masonic journey, and I’m grateful for your guidance and for setting
an example for me to emulate. I also want to thank Liz for her unconditional
support over the past 31 years and for being with me on this journey.
As a former Army officer, leadership is an important fundamental to me.
This year, my theme is “Crafting Leadership—in Ourselves, in Our Lodges,
and in Our Communities.” I see opportunities for us to change ourselves by
applying our principles in daily life, in our lodges by engaging our brethren in
new and meaningful ways, and in our communities by being active and involved
in making positive changes.
Our emblem of the beehive brings out how we make the theme come
alive. We know the beehive well from our ritual, and it relates to us all to a
core principle of showing up and working hard. The bees are arranged in sets
of three, five, and seven to remind us that leadership is found throughout our
Craft and in our Entered Apprentices, Fellow Crafts, and Master Masons. The
butterfly, or “flutterby,” represents that our spouses and partners can also play
a critical leadership role as we work together to make a positive change in our
communities. As the bees and butterfly are the pollinators in nature, we have the
opportunity to serve as social pollinators this year. The image of the hive is that
from the inside, and it is our goal to get outside of our hive, or lodge, and into
the community to work. By showing up and working hard, by being ourselves,
and by living our values, we will be examples of leadership within our Craft

78

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

and in our communities. Together we can help transform society as a whole.
Crafting Leadership in Ourselves: In ourselves, we should strive to be
our best and to live our tenets and to practice the four cardinal virtues. We
should not just learn our ritual and lectures but apply the working tools in our
daily lives. In our daily lives, where we live, work, and play, I ask that we speak
to everyone about Masonry, and, if absolutely necessary, we should use our
words. But showing up and working hard for constant self-improvement will
be revealed by your actions and have a more lasting impact than anything we
say. When we do have something to say, we can talk about what Masonry means
to us as individuals, how we have formed bonds of fellowship within the lodge
that are truly transformational and life changing.
Crafting Leadership in Our Lodges: In our lodges, our Master and
Wardens provide the leadership, vision, and guidance to bring our fraternity’s
2025 Strategic Plan to life. Our Inspectors play the crucial role of supporting
the lodge leadership. Within our lodges, I am seeking to inspire the leadership
to create programs to promote our members’ engagement, which gives them
a purpose and a sense of belonging. We can start by asking the brethren what
they want to see within their lodge. That leadership within the lodge helps us
build that special place where we can nourish our unique friendships. We can
provide all our members and families with a sense of belonging and purpose
with engaging activities for learning and fellowship. We have opportunities to
strengthen the foundation of our lodge, and then to transform our lodge into
the cornerstone of the community.
Crafting Leadership in Our communities: In our communities, we have
leadership opportunities that are unbounded. I see our time this year not just
focused on our personal Masonic journeys or inside our lodges. I see us reaching
out to the community and being an active part in changing our society. We can
be the example of leadership within our communities.
I see our engagement with our community starting with our relationship
with community leaders. Inviting our civic leaders, educators, and civic organization leaders to our public lodge events is the first step in building strong
relationships within the community. Once we know each other, we can then
ask what we can do to support the community in which we live. We will then be
able to understand what the community needs from us. That could be hosting
events in our lodge, such as sponsoring Red Cross blood donations, becoming an
election day polling place, or hosting community events in which our members
engage the community leadership. The key is to partner with the community
and to be able to provide our leadership to support the towns and cities where
we live. This will promote that positive awareness of Masons as being active and
supportive of the community and demonstrate our Masonic values in action.
By showing our communities what we have to offer, by inviting them into
our lodges to have open discussions about what we do and what it means to us,
we will create that interest that will have men knocking at our doors looking
for what we have. When we are in dialogue with our community leaders, we

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

79

will also understand their view of leadership within the community and how
they see our role in society.
We already have strong relationships within our schools through our Public
Schools Advisory Committees and from our engagement via the Raising A Reader
program. Working with educational leadership as a lodge or as individual brothers supports free public education within our community and the betterment
of society. In supporting Raising A Reader, we support early childhood literacy
and can make a positive impact on our future generations today.
As we can be active in the communities where we live and work, we can also
be active in our greater Masonic community. Working closely with our entire
Masonic family projects a united picture of California Freemasonry to our communities. When they see Shriners in a parade, our Scottish Rite language centers,
or our Eastern Star Chapter at a Relay for Life, they will know that we are all
part of one Masonic family making a positive impact on our local community.
I also see an important role for us in supporting the future leaders within
our Masonic family. Find ways to connect with the DeMolay chapter, the Jobs
Daughters bethel, or the Rainbow assembly in your area. Support their engagement within the community with your leadership, financial support, and active
participation. Find a way to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the International
Order of the Rainbow for Girls with your local assembly and make it a big celebration for the entire Masonic community. This is near and dear to me, as both
my daughters were active in Rainbow, and Liz and I were active in our assembly
as advisers. Along with Job’s Daughters and DeMolay, I look for us to support
our youth orders with your presence at their events. They need our leadership
to keep their assemblies, bethels, and chapters running. We may even be able
to learn from their leadership!
When we work within our local communities, reach out to the local Prince
Hall Lodge to see how we can find common ground, to learn about each other,
and to align on ways to coordinate our good works within the community.
When our community thinks of Masons and Masonry, we need to recognize
that they are looking at all of us. Everyone wearing a Masonic ring, sporting
a lodge polo at an event, or proudly displaying a Square and Compass sticker
on their car is providing the community an example of who we are as Masons
and of what we do.
Lastly, Liz and I are strong advocates for our Masonic Center for Youth and
Families. This not-for-profit service of the Masonic Homes of California offers
therapeutic services for children, adolescents, young adults, and their families.
It is a clear demonstration of our Masonic values and an embodiment of our
commitment to the belief that all young people should be empowered to realize
their full potential. This year we will support events and get the word out to
our brethren and families of this important service. We will also highlight the
impact on Masonic families and on the local communities.
In closing, we as Masons or as members of a Masonic family can make a
difference in our communities through our individual and collective efforts.

80

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

This takes showing up and hard work. We are like that bee out there collecting
pollen and working away, and in the process pollinating the flowers and trees,
enabling them to bear fruit in due season. I see our lodges and us in a similar
way within our communities, providing the “pollination” of society. As we
focus on our self-improvement as Masons, that effort can improve the society
of which we are members. That showing up and working hard to be a servant
in our community, in our lodge, in our homes, is the leadership I am looking
to inspire this year.
I thank you all for being here today for this special occasion and for being
part of this Grand Lodge installation ceremony. I thank the brethren of California
for their trust and faith in me. I am grateful for the opportunity to serve our
beloved Craft as our Grand Master of Masons in California. I’m proud to be
here today and honored to serve you in the year to come with reliance upon
our Supreme Grand Master’s help, guidance, and support.

REPORT OF THE
SENIOR GRAND WARDEN
2021-2022 PER CAPITA PROPOSAL
Randall L. Brill, Senior Grand Warden

Dear Brethren,
As senior grand warden, it is my pleasure to present to you the per capita
proposal which will fund the Grand Lodge budget during the fiscal year of
November 1, 2022 through October 31, 2023. This per capita will be collected
next summer based on the number of Masons on the rolls of each lodge on
June 30, 2022.
As you are aware, the COVID-19 pandemic continues to impact our financial
planning. I’m grateful to have worked with our Deputy Grand Master and others
over the past year to build a solid financial plan despite the many challenges we
face. Our goal has been to maintain services and programs, provide resources
for our strategic objectives, and do so without putting the burden on per capita
paid by our lodges, which face similar challenges.
As explained at the Annual Communication last year, operating reserves
from the Nob Hill Masonic Center and the Grand Lodge operating surplus from
the 2020 fiscal year and the current one will allow us to meet these objectives.
Though the per capita multiplier will grow, the increase will cover normal
operating cost increases but not impacts created by the pandemic. As we plan
to operate within 2022–23, the strategic use of our reserves makes this possible.
Further, I expect that we will have a strong year in membership as lodges work
through a backlog of applications and degrees. We have the opportunity to at
least maintain membership levels, if not grow.
The multiplier will increase based on the following factors:
1. Labor expenses will increase by 3.7 percent, including health benefits,
which represents $71,393 in additional cost, or approximately $1.83 in
per capita.
2. Nonlabor expenses subject to normal inflation will increase by 2 percent. Fraternal and Appropriations will also increase by 2 percent.
These areas represent $34,643, or $0.89 in per capita.

84

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

3.

Lodge insurance costs will increase by 7 percent, which represents
$0.24 in per capita.
Taken together, these factors would require us to increase per capita by
$2.96. However, other areas will reduce this amount. An increase in investment
and other income, a decrease in contingency, a small increase in membership,
and an increase of $5,000 in operating reserves represent $0.71 of reduced per
capita. Therefore, the per capita I propose for the 2023 fiscal year is $57.50.
Despite the challenging times we have all endured over the past year, I am
optimistic about the r fraternity. I am excited about our vision for the future
and our 2025 Plan. With your support of this proposal, we will continue our
important programs and services, including new lodge development, leadership
training, communications, technology, financial and administrative programs,
and the initiatives to increase positive public awareness and membership growth.
As we continue to work together closer and in harmony, we will fulfill our
obligations as Masons, and lay the foundation for a strong future in which our
members proudly discuss the fraternity, lodges engage with their communities,
and we are known for our good work.
Thank you for your support!
Sincerely and fraternally,
Randall L. Brill, Senior Grand Warden

REPORT OF THE
GRAND TREASURER
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren All,
In this my sixth and final address to you as Grand Treasurer, I am pleased
to report to you that despite the continued economic challenges presented by
COVID-19, the financial health of our Grand Lodge and related entities remains
strong. We benefit from the efforts and expertise of many brothers who continue to volunteer their time as board members and committee members, and
the expertise of our entire Grand Lodge financial team, led by Tom Boyer, our
CFO; Maribel Pasamic, our Controller; Khalil Sweidy, our Director of Financial
Planning and Real Estate; and, of course, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, our
Grand Secretary.
The Audit Committee, led by Worshipful Tony Garcia, has again chosen to
continue our engagement with Moss Adams as our outside auditor, to ensure
that our financial-statement audits for all our Grand Lodge entities continues
to go smoothly. As of our last fiscal year ending October 31, 2020, each of our
entities again received a clean audit opinion, and were informed that our internal controls remain effective and that our model for shared service costs is not
only appropriate but consistent with best practices and industry standards.
The Finance Committee, led by Worshipful Levon Keshishian, continues
to bring their broad corporate experience to our budgeting process in working with our Deputy Grand Master and Senior Grand Warden to provide wise
and timely counsel in the preparation of their annual budgets and per capita
determinations.
The Insurance Committee, led by Worshipful David Forsyth, continues
their tireless work in their detailed review of our complex insurance needs not
only for our Grand Lodge entities but also for our lodges and Hall Associations.
This includes an ongoing review of claims to ensure an optimal result for the
benefit of the craft and to look for ways to do all of this in the most cost-efficient
manner possible, particularly in an environment where insurance premiums
are constantly rising.
The Investments Committee, led by Worshipful Wil Smith, continues their
in-depth analysis of the economic factors that impact our portfolio. In their
ongoing evaluation of our investment policies, they recommend that 4.5 percent

92

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

of our investment portfolio be distributed to fund the Grand Lodge operating
budget. The relationship with NEPC, our investment advisory firm, which is
now in its fourth year, continues to bring forth meaningful discussions with our
fund managers and provide a deeper dive on our asset allocations.
The following financial highlights are based on unaudited results for the
nine-month period through July 31, 2021, compared with the audited results
from October 31, 2020. The audited financial statements for the current fiscal
year ending October 31, 2021 will be made available with these annual proceedings upon publication.

I have reported the various changes to the investments of each of our
entities, but it should also be noted that, in aggregate, our Master Trust has
increased $190,922,876, or 19 percent, net of distributions for the operations for
all of our entities, including the costs of construction at both Masonic Homes
campuses. The Master Trust now stands at $1,193,592,771 as of July 31, 2021.
The breakdown of the Master Trust per entity is as follows:
• Masonic Homes in the amount of $1,088,197,328, or 91.2 percent
• California Masonic Foundation in the amount of $45,883,215, or 3.8
percent
• Acacia Creek in the amount of $22,733,491, or 1.9 percent
• California Masonic Memorial Temple in the amount of $4,970,024, or
0.4 percent
• Grand Lodge in the amount of $14,164,667, or 1.2 percent
• Lodge Investment Program in the amount of $14,287,919, or 1.2
percent
• Lodge Life Membership Program in the amount of $2,703,826, or 0.2
percent
• Nob Hill Masonic Center in the amount of $652,301, or 0.1 percent
The return on investment for the year to date is 25.8 percent, and since
inception of our Master Trust in 1995 it remains at a healthy 8 percent.
While our Master Trust continues to grow, we must remember that these
funds are not available to simply withdraw to cover the expenses of each of our
entities. As I previously mentioned, we are limited to draw 4.5 percent of the
five-year average of the investments for each entity to support the operations.
This means that in the example of our Masonic Homes, with a current operating budget of approximately $65 million and an investment distribution of
approximately $37 million, we have a delta of approximately $28 million dollars
that needs to be made up from other sources such as fees for certain services
and each of our annual contributions in fulfillment of our ongoing obligations
to each other.
In 1992, our Grand Lodge created an Endowment Fund to be funded
each year by the budget surpluses of each Grand Master. Since that time, the
Endowment Fund has grown to $3,092,054 as of July 31, 2021. As I mentioned
earlier, this year we will again be accruing the surplus as a deferred asset for
operating reserves to normalize the budgets and per capita assessments over
the next several years due to the economic impacts of COVID-19 on our operations at Nob Hill Masonic Center and the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
This same Endowment Fund will now provide $110,935 for the budget of Right
Worshipful Wilkins in the fiscal year ending October 31, 2022, compared with

96

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

$107,898 for the current fiscal year.
Participation in the Grand Lodge Life Membership Funds and the Grand
Lodge General Investments Fund has increased over the past year, providing
lodges a much-needed option in their investment strategies. As of July 31,
2021, we have 56 lodges participating in the Life Membership Master Fund,
with a value of $2,703,826, and we have 24 lodges participating in the Lodge
Investments Master Fund, with a value of $14,287,919. As we continue to move
forward into our suite of online services with iMember 2.0 and Intacct, I would
like to encourage our lodge officers and Hall Association directors to take
full advantage of the expertise of our Grand Lodge Finance Team with budgets, investments, payroll matters, tax filings, real estate matters, and general
accounting matters. In utilizing these services and their expertise, you will be
able to focus more of your attention on practicing Masonry within your lodge
and your community.
I would also like to encourage you to begin lodge budget discussions as
early as possible with the key people in your lodge, such as your prospective
wardens, treasurer, secretary, trustees, Hall Association directors, and those with
experience in such matters. Discuss your budgets openly and frequently so that
the finances of your lodge do not become one of the mysteries of Freemasonry.
Lastly, I would like to say that it has been a great honor to serve as the 23rd
Grand Treasurer for our Grand Lodge. Thank you, Most Worshipful Weiss, along
with Most Worshipfuls Perry, Heisner, Galloway, Wright, and Trauner, for your
trust and friendship, and all of you, my brothers, for having blessed me with this
opportunity. And thank you to my dear friend Very Worshipful Allan Casalou.
Your business knowledge and passion for our Craft have made these past six
years a wonderful experience for me personally, and I know our Grand Lodge
operations are in highly capable hands.
Respectfully submitted,
Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Grand Treasurer

REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to make this, my 14th report as your Grand Secretary. I am
elated to be standing here surrounded by you in our memorial temple. In has
been a challenging 18 months for everyone. But here we are, together again to
conduct our annual business and demonstrate once more that Freemasonry,
notwithstanding, still survives.

Membership Information
Current Membership Statistics
As of June 30, 2021, we had 42,037 active Masons, including 2,795 Entered
Apprentice Masons and 886 Fellow Crafts. Our Masonic family also includes
14,066 widows. Please refer to my written report for detailed membership
activity, bylaw amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards.
PROGRAMS AND SERVICES
Led by the 2025 Fraternity Plan, the focus of the Grand Lodge office is to
provide quality services and programs, which reduce administrative burdens
and prioritize the member experience. As this pandemic has continued, we
have enhanced our virtual programming skills and honed our virtual service
capabilities while working with you to reopen and reinvigorate our fraternity.
iMember 2.0
In July 2020, we partnered with GrandView Systems to roll out iMember 2.0
and advanced a growing movement of collaboration. More than 50 other grand
lodges and Masonic organizations around the globe are now using GrandView,
including those nearby such as the Grand Chapter of California, Order of the
Eastern Star, Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Grand Lodge of Oregon,

100

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Grand Lodge of Washington, and Grand lodge of Nevada. The list also includes
grand lodges in North America, Africa, and Australia; Masonic organizations
like the Red Cross of Constantine also use GrandView. We are now part of an
international collaboration never known before in Freemasonry. As we work
together to refine the system, we are learning from each other and bringing this
world-wide fraternity closer and closer together.
Today, 40 percent of California Masons have personally registered on
iMember 2.0, gaining access to their member record and virtual dues card, lodge
rosters, Masonic education, and other resources. iMember 2.0 will continue to
evolve and improve. I’m grateful to our lodge leaders, and particularly lodge
secretaries and assistant secretaries, who have embraced this new system and
provided invaluable feedback and recommendations to improve it.
Dues Payment Service
Before this year, secretaries and assistant secretaries spent an average of six
months of the year invoicing, collecting, and processing dues payments. This is
valuable time that these officers could spend on other important duties, such
as communicating with prospects, members, and widows. Also, more and more
members were being suspended for nonpayment of dues. Immediately following
the virtual Annual Communication in 2020, we launched our first statewide dues
service. There are two goals of this service. First, to reduce the administrative
burden of the secretary, and second, to make it easier for members to pay their
dues and receive their dues card. More than two-thirds of our lodges opted into
this voluntary program. The Grand Lodge sent dues notices to the members
of participating lodges, collected their payments—which included a high percentage of credit card payments—updated the member record, and provided
a dues card. The Grand Lodge made three follow-up notices to members who
had not paid before sending the list of nonpayments to the lodge for follow-up.
Additionally, 10 percent of our members belong to more than one lodge.
They received a single invoice and were able to pay dues to all their lodges in
one payment transaction. Grand Lodge sent each lodge 100 percent of the dues
collected on a regular basis. The service was provided without any additional
fees. Dues payments from more than 26,000 members were received through
this program. We made significant progress with members who had been in
arrears. More than 1,300 members who were subject to suspension for nonpayment of dues paid their current and prior years’ dues through this program
and sustained their lodge membership. Lodges participating in the grand lodge
dues service collected payments from 20 percent more members than lodges
who did not participate. These are the results we can achieve when our lodges
and our Grand Lodge work together.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

101

Member Services
Our Member Services team provides core support to lodges and members
with services and programs. They processed more than 11,700 information and
service requests this year, a 16 percent increase from last year, completing more
than 90 percent on the first day with an average completion time of 150 minutes.
The Masonic Speaker Series continues to connect Masons in California and
around the world on a wide variety of topics, from the esoteric and contemplative, such as Dr. Michael Coughlin’s excellent address entitled “From Mythos
to Logos: Andrea Palladio, Freemasonry, and the Triumph of Minerva,” to the
practical, with presentations similar to our own Most Worshipful Brother Russ
Charvonia’s address on our role in restoring civility to society.
We hosted the ninth International Conference on Freemasonry online in
March, with more than 900 attendees from around the globe. We plan to continue to make use of a hybrid event, bringing together scholars and Masons in
person in April 2022 while connecting with a broader international audience to
continue to share this excellent program that encourages original scholarship
on Freemasonry with the world. Additionally, we hosted the annual California
Masonic Symposium online for the second year, again with a record audience
that continues to underscore the power of virtual events.
More than 700 lodge leaders participated in our leadership retreats this
year. Secretaries and Treasurers sessions were held virtually. As COVID-19
restrictions relaxed earlier this year, we held our first in-person event in over
a year on June 11, the Master and Warden’s Retreat in Irvine. Later we held the
same retreat in San Ramon. Similar training was provided online for those who
could not attend in person. We held two in-person Inspectors Retreats, one in
August and one in September.
We were pleased to support the Grand Master’s Liberty Tour to Philadelphia
in August. The Grand Master and 80 other brothers and family members traveled to the City of Brotherly Love to explore the origins of our country and the
Masonic impact on America. We received wonderful hospitality from the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania, which has one of the most beautiful Masonic Temples
in the world. We’re so pleased to have their Grand Master and other Grand
Lodge officers with us this weekend, including my colleague Right Worshipful
Brother Mark Haines, the Grand Secretary. The tour was completed safely,
and everyone had a wonderful time. I want to thank Jose Camello, Worshipful
Brother Jonathan Prestage, Billy Lynam, and our entire communications team,
who worked so well together to provide the logistics for this event.
New Lodge Development
Our efforts in new lodge development continue to grow. Since the beginning
of this initiative, 30 new lodges have been instituted. Four were instituted this
year, making a total of nine lodges under dispensation. I will give a full report
on charters tomorrow.

102

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Financial Services
The Financial Services team provides accounting, budgeting, reporting,
and audit support for Grand Lodge and our related entities. Additionally, they
provide a variety of supportive programs and resources for lodges and halls.
Our latest financial service to lodges and halls was the implementation of
Paychex. Financial services trained and onboarded 98 lodges and 23 halls to
this new payroll program this year.
Grand Master Weiss incorporated the full cost of our accounting software
for lodges in this year’s budget. Today, nearly 80 percent of lodges and 60 percent of halls are using Intacct as their accounting solution and are receiving
high-quality service from the grand lodge finance team.
This year, Financial Services prepared and filed 583 tax returns for lodges,
hall associations, and residents of the Masonic Homes.
For the 12th year, the audits of the six entities of the Masons of California
were completed with no audit adjustments, disagreements with management,
or weaknesses in internal controls noted by Moss Adams, our outside auditor,
in its annual report to the boards.
Real Estate Services
Our real estate services team provided a full complement of property-related services to our lodges and halls, and maintained the several Grand Lodgeowned properties. The team led renovations at Benicia Masonic Hall, the first
Masonic building in California, which will be completed this year. Refurbishment
of the Quitman Masonic Building in Malakoff Diggins State Park is underway.
Upon completion, it will be yet another historic California hall we’ve preserved.
The Grand Lodge maintains two masonic cemeteries related to the
Columbia Masonic Hall in Columbia State Park, the Columbia Masonic cemetery and the Jamestown Masonic cemetery. We have obtained a comprehensive
conditions assessment report for the maintenance and restoration of these
historic properties.
Masonic Mediation
As Grand Secretary, I am responsible for the administration of Masonic
Trials, and I have the assistance of our legal team to support this work. Among
his Grand Master’s Recommendations in 2019, Most Worshipful Brother Wright
established a Masonic mediation process for navigating charges filed against
another Mason if, in the opinion of the jurisprudence committee, the charges warranted pretrial mediation. This mediation process was finalized in 2021 and has
resulted in numerous matters being settled without the need of a Masonic trial.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

103

Communications
Our Communications team executes a comprehensive communications
strategy for our fraternity through websites, social media, email, a monthly
leadership e-newsletter, and California Freemason magazine, which once again
received national awards in the publishing industry.
For the 17th straight year, our magazine won national awards from the
Association of Media and Publishing, including the gold award for magazine
redesign, recognizing the new editorial and design strategy of the magazine.
We received the bronze award for best single-topic issue for the “Eye of the
Storm” issue, which dealt with COVID-19 and the fire emergency response by
the fraternity.
These awards will mark another year in which our internal communications
team beat out agencies that are dedicated to publishing magazines for membership organizations. Our design and editorial accomplishments continue to
lead the pack in the nonprofit and membership sectors.
This year, leveraging our internal communications team’s talent, we brought
the design of the magazine in-house, meaning that the entirety of California
Freemason, from editorial to design, is produced by us. We also launched an
online subscription service, which has over 150 new subscribers.
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
It is my responsibility to inform the Grand Master of matters pertaining to
foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in the form of a motion,
the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet our criteria. The Grand Lodge
has received the following requests for recognition by foreign grand lodges.
1. Lithuania. The Grand Lodge of Lithuania was established in 2002 by
the United Grand Lodges of Germany. It has six lodges. In 2005, the
Commission on Information for Recognition determined that this
Grand Lodge promotes the tenets and customs of the Craft and practices regular Masonry.
2. Brazil. In Brazil there is a national Grand Orient, a separate confederation of 27 State Grand Lodges, and a number of independent State
Grand Orients, which are separate and sovereign from the national
Grand Orient. Our Grand Lodge currently recognizes the Grand
Orient of Brazil and all 27 State Grand Lodges. We have received a
request from the Grand Orient of Rio de Janeiro, which was formed
in 1974, has 65 lodges, is a member of the Inter-American Masonic
Confederation, and enjoys mutual recognition with the two other
Grand Lodges in the same territory that we recognize. In 2020, the
commission reported that this state grand orient is in amity with the
other Grand Lodges where they share territory.

104

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

In reviewing their applications, we find that both Grand Lodges are regular
and meet the standards of recognition of our Grand Lodge.
The Grand Secretary moved that the Grand Lodge of California approve the
petitions and grant mutual recognition with the Grand Lodge of Lithuania and
the Grand Orient of Rio de Janeiro. The Grand Lecturer seconded the motion
and the motion was adopted.
GRAND SECRETARY
The Grand Lodge of California has requested mutual recognition with
all Prince Hall Grand Lodges in the U.S. and elsewhere that maintain mutual
recognition with a Grand Lodge in their jurisdiction that is already recognized
by the Grand Lodge of California, if one exists. The Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of
the State of Tennessee and the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of
Tennessee have entered into an agreement of mutual recognition. This Prince
Hall Grand Lodge was founded in 1870 and is a member of the Conference of
Grand Masters Prince Hall Masons Inc.
The Grand Secretary moved that the Grand Lodge of California approve
the petitions and grant mutual recognition with the Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of Tennessee. The Grand Lecturer seconded the motion and the motion was
adopted.
APPRECIATION
As I conclude my report, I extend my sincere gratitude to the lodge secretaries
and assistant secretaries whose dedicated work is the backbone of our jurisdiction. I also thank our Assistant Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors who,
in addition to their ritual duties, provide invaluable administrative support
throughout the year.
I am blessed to have had the opportunity to work with our Grand Treasurer,
Very Worshipful Brother Art Salazar. He is a dear brother, a good friend, and
an excellent colleague. His service as Grand Treasurer will be remembered for
his capable leadership and kind spirit. Thank you, my brother, for your service
and your friendship.
We also appreciate the team of true professionals in our Grand Lodge office,
all of whom care deeply about our fraternity and support our mission with
their dedicated service. I thank them all for their commitment and good work.
Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother Arthur
H. Weiss, whose strong vision for our fraternity has guided us through this past
year. When faced with adversity, our Grand Master relied on this vision to call
us to our greatest selves, to come together and move our fraternity forward.
There is a quote displayed at the Ronald Regan Presidential Library in Southern
California, where Barbara Weiss is a docent, that comes to mind when I think
of our Grand Master. President Reagan said, “The greatest leader is not necessarily the one who does the greatest things. He is the one that gets the people

to do the greatest things.” Looking back at this year, I say our Grand Master
has lived up to this definition. He has challenged us and inspired us to carry the
fraternity toward the 2050 vision of “The World in Harmony.” Thank you, Most
Worshipful, for your vision, your leadership, and your friendship.
And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

REPORT ON LODGE CHARTERS
AND DISPENSATIONS
By Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary
In accordance with Section 801.065 of the California Masonic Code, the
following lodges have petitioned this Grand Lodge for a charter.
• Benicia Lodge U.D. in Benicia. Past Grand Master Perry granted a
dispensation to Benicia Lodge on October 20, 2016.
• The Thirty-Three Lodge U.D. in Irvine. Past Grand Master Trauner
granted a dispensation to The Thirty-Three Lodge on September 10,
2020.
• Columbia Historic Lodge U.D. in Columbia. Past Grand Master
Trauner granted a dispensation to Columbia Historic Lodge on
October 1, 2020.
In reviewing the records of these lodges, and from the information provided
by the Inspectors and Assistant Grand Lecturers, it has been determined that
these lodges meet the requirements of the petition.
A motion was made, seconded, and adopted to issue the following charters:
• Benicia Lodge No. 877
• The Thirty-Three Lodge No. 878
• Columbia Historic Lodge
The Grand Master issued dispensations to the following lodges:
• Andres Bonifacio Lodge U.D. in Gardena on April 14, 2021
• Ye Olde Cup & Ball Lodge U.D. in Newport Beach on June 28, 2021
• Seven Hills Lodge U.D. in San Francisco on July 26, 2021
• GAT Jose Rizal Lodge U.D. in Menifee on August 8, 2021
On August 2, 2021, Riverside Lodge No. 635 voted to voluntarily surrender
its charter.

112

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

It was moved and seconded that the voluntary surrender of the charter
issued to Riverside Lodge No. 635 be accepted by the Grand Lodge, and that
the lodge be dissolved in accordance with the code. The motion was adopted.
On June 19, 2019, the charter for Van Nuys Lodge No. 450 was suspended
and arrested.
It was moved and seconded that the Charter issued to Van Nuys Lodge No.
450 be revoked, that the lodge be dissolved in accordance with the Code, and
that the assets thereof, other than the lodge’s Life Membership Fund, be held
for the furtherance of Freemasonry in the San Fernando Valley. The motion
was not adopted.

REPORT OF THE
GRAND LECTURER
I. Looking Back into the Past
Brethren all,
This is my third report to you my brethren as your Grand Lecturer.
I take great pleasure today looking out into our Grand Lodge auditorium
to see my brethren sitting together in our Masonic house on Nob Hill. I have a
renewed appreciation for the privilege of being able to sit in lodge again with
my brothers. I believe it harms the soul when we are forced to be apart from
one another, and I hope you, too, have found that appreciation and will always
remember what it felt like not to be together.
In years to come, when we are able to take off these masks and tell the
stories of how we arrived at this place in dealing with this pandemic—the
restrictions, the shutdowns, the isolation, constant reports of the numbers
of people inflicted and hospitalized or dying—I hope we also remember the
stories of our members and lodges rising above the rhetoric and opening their
hearts to those with great needs, goods and meals donated and distributed in
lodge parking lots, and brothers checking up on one another and addressing
their needs as well.
Last year in my video report to you, my brethren, I stated that in spite of
the promising start we had to the 2019–20 Grand Lodge year, it pained me to
report that there was no Ritual being performed in California. The hope of
returning to our lodges and opening back up by Memorial Day weekend 2020
came and went. Little did we realize then that we would have to wait at least 12
more long months. During those 12 months, we documented our observations
and the actions we took. We made use of the tools and resources at our disposal.
We tried to extract from the past every ounce of information that was useful
to our circumstances in light of what was happening in the world around us.
Then there was the technology: the Zoom meetings, the educational forums,
the training sessions, and the toasts. These allowed for some form of social
interaction. The technology helped, but it wasn’t quite enough. We still longed
to be in person. We found that Zoom was quite effective in the performance of
our constitution ceremonies. We began to use the term “virtual.” We discovered

126

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

a new position—virtual coordinator. And speaking of virtual coordination, at
this time I wish to give my thanks to Wor. Mike Ramos, and to Brothers Marty
Cusing and Jonathan Cornn, for all your time and valuable assistance to the
Craft. The real challenges came when we began to address virtual lodge installations. With much discussion, we eventually found that addressing changes to
virtual floor work and instructions were all that was required to proceed while
leaving the Ritual of our installations intact. This got us into February. Next
came several lodge institutions. With these we needed only to follow what we
had already learned in performing our virtual constitutions. A few more virtual stated meetings and Masonic education forums and were looking at the
beginning of May 2021.

Condition of the Ritual in California
We have had a front-row seat to watch these events unfold and to see the reactions of our brethren to the needs of the Craft and our communities. With Grand
Master Weiss’s April 14, 2021 Reopening Directive, we were not seeing our lodges
opening quickly. It was not as we had anticipated an opening in May of 2020
would have looked. The gradual opening of our lodges and the slow increase
in activity looked more like a bear waking up from a long hibernation. But the
lodges did open. First came the in-person stated meetings with masks, then the
much-anticipated degrees. The Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors were
contacting their lodges to determine which degree was the priority for their
lodge and to begin the process of rehearsing. In many cases, the Inspectors were
having to requalify officers to ensure Ritual quality after such a long hiatus. I
attended a third-degree performance at Chico-Leland Stanford Lodge on July
6. This was their second third degree since the reopening. I appreciated the
invitation from their Lodge Master, Worshipful John Barneson, to attend and
enjoyed my first third degree in 18 months. I observed my own lodge in Elk
Grove take giant steps to renewing the officer Ritual proficiencies by taking
advantage of the time after we reopened to begin working together and to return
to fellowship in person. Their first attempt at restarting the Ritual came at our
June 2021 stated meeting. The first degree opening was very rough, but the jewel
march showed promise. As it turned out, we discovered that maintaining the
six-foot minimal distance between brethren actually improved the jewel march!
The two newly appointed Elk Grove officers coaches, Worshipful Darryl Watts
and Worshipful Justin Gingery, had little time and wasted none of it trying
to help their lodge officers deliver quality work. I observed the fruit of those
labors in the performance of an outstanding and meaningful double Entered
Apprentice degree on June 17. I equate my observations of these two officers’
coaches to coming up for their very first at-bat with bases loaded and hitting a
grand slam on opening day. In the short time we have had to prepare after the

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

127

reopening, I am very appreciative to the masters, wardens, and officers coaches
from Burbank Lodge for allowing me to attend their third-degree rehearsal of
September 23, and the Inspector and officers of District 636 for allowing me to
visit their reopening district School of Instruction of September 24. I am especially appreciative for the officers and members of Maya Lodge No. 793 and Logia
Panamericana No. 513 for allowing me to attend my first performance of the
Spanish-language third degree on September 30. Mi hermanos, your degree work
was beautiful and meaningful. Thank you for an evening of sincere friendship
and fellowship. With these strong and meaningful examples, and the reports I
have received from our Assistant Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors, it is
my pleasure to report to you at this time that after 18 long months, our Ritual
has returned in California.
Status of Music
Four years ago, we began a venture to restore music to each of our lodges. This
has given Steve Miller, our Grand Organist, and me the opportunity to reach
out to our lodge organists and begin the conversation. We all have a rhythm.
But each of our rhythms is unique and not always in sync with those around us,
especially when we are performing our Ritual. When the appropriate music is
played within our lodges, the rhythm of the music brings us together; it gives
meaning and enhances the experience. The pandemic has gotten in the way of
continuing this project. Earlier last year we began making arrangements to visit
our Masonic Homes and ask the residents who could play a musical instrument
to prepare and allow us to record their music, to be placed on our website. We
were optimistic that we could do it this summer, but the surge in the delta
variant has interfered with our efforts once again.
Steve and I wish to thank Worshipful Christopher Smith, our Grand Lodge
Director of IT, for helping to move the project forward, from the Inspectors
files to the member side to the public side of our website for downloads. We are
grateful to Emily Limon and her team at Grand Lodge Communications for the
transfer and setting up of the web location in the public side of freemason.org,
and identifying the 2025 Strategic Plan worthiness of this project. My continual
thanks and appreciation to Dr. Joseph Pritchard and Kim Hegg at our Masonic
Home in Union City for beginning the process of working with our residents
to record and save their talents for others to enjoy.
Worshipful Al and Worshipful Charles
This year I have had the privilege to serve with nine very different and insightful
brothers who have worked together in your Ritual Committee. Each of us have
brought to the committee different backgrounds and experiences, but we all
have at least one thing in common: the protection of consistent and meaningful
Ritual in California. Two of our members are completing their service to the
committee as Assistant Grand Lecturers—Worshipful Charles Cross in Division

128

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

VI, and Worshipful Elvan Moen in Division VII. My brethren, I have treasured
the time we have spent together and the work we have accomplished. Each of
you are an outstanding example of brotherly and Masonic character. Patty and
I wish to convey our love to you Al and Lori, and to you Charles and Sandra,
for your fellowship and friendship. Brethren, please join me in thanking these
two exemplary Masons!
I take great pleasure in welcoming our two new Assistant Grand Lecturers
taking over the administrative and Ritual management of their respective divisions, Worshipful Matthew Vander Horck, a Past Master of Long Beach Lodge
No. 327 and the Inspector of the 642nd Masonic District, will be taking over in
Division VI, and Worshipful Alberto Casanova, a Past Master of San Fernando
Lodge No. 343 and Inspector of the 705th Masonic District, will be taking over
in Division VII. Welcome, my brothers, to the Ritual Committee.
A Return of Ritual Competition for 2022
Another casualty of the year was our planned Ritual Competition 2021. The
Ritual Committee had it set up for implementation once we were given the
green light to meet. But due to the lateness of the year, it was determined
that the Inspectors and AGLs would not have the time necessary to provide a
meaningful competition. However, I have it on good authority that there will be
a competition next year. Please stay posted for information following Annual
Communication.
Thank You for Allowing Me to Serve

GRAND CHAPLAIN’S MESSAGE
“A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for a time of adversity.”
Some biblical verses are just timeless, aren’t they? This verse can be found in
Proverbs 17:17. And I’d like to begin by thanking you for inspiring me. We have
certainly experienced a time of adversity together since the beginning of the
pandemic. Much like the way we are taught to accept new members into our
Fraternity, this verse discusses the transition of a friend to a brother. A brother
is someone who is bonded to us, in our Fraternity through common ritual and
the obligations we take to one another and mankind. But before I get too much
further, I am aware that today’s session is open, so it should go without saying
that this shared experience is no doubt similar for those of you in the women’s
orders and youth orders, among others. I am speaking from my viewpoint as
a Mason in the Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons, and so I am going to
say “brother” a lot!
I don’t need to remind you how we were compelled to end in-person gatherings and thrust into the virtual world of Zoom, because you all experienced
it. And I don’t want to remind you of the many tragedies of the past year, the
pain of loss, the friends and mentors who are no longer with us—this is, after
all, supposed to be an inspirational message!
But I do want to remind you that over the past countless months you proved
you were brothers for a time of adversity. You heeded the call when you came to
the aid of your Masonic family through your own personal endeavors, together
with your lodges, or by rising to the occasion and donating to the Distressed
Worthy Brother Fund at the California Masonic Foundation, which has been
one of the most successful campaigns in the history of our fraternity.
And you didn’t stop there, did you? Many of you provided refreshment to
your Masonic family as they sheltered in place, which was far more than a meal.
It was your smiling eyes—you were wearing a mask, after all—and your laughter
that truly nourished your brothers. Thank you for inspiring me.
I’d like to share some other inspiring people and moments during my time
as your Grand Chaplain.
Worshipful Chris Veres, Master of Santa Barbara No. 192, for his pandemic
activity of keeping a journal reflecting on Brother Benjamin Franklin and his 13
virtues. For those of you not familiar with Brother Franklin’s virtues, you are
encouraged to read about them, as there isn’t time for me to go through them
today. And Worshipful Veres, I look forward to hearing how the activity went.

GRAND ORATION
How good does it feel to be here in person at Annual Communication?
Has anybody ever put thought into what this world would look like if
Freemasonry didn’t exist? Would the world, in particular the United States,
look the same? Would there be a Declaration of Independence? Would we still
be a territory of Great Britain?
Our gentle Craft was the first of its kind to teach religious tolerance and
liberty. Had Masonic lodges not been present in Philadelphia, when many of the
ideas for this document were being discussed, would the men have been tolerant
enough with one another to have formed such an important document. While
this time in history is significant, for generations, the teachings of Freemasonry
have played a monumental role in shaping the United States as we know it today.
Good morning! My name is Michael Thibodeaux, and I am a seventh-generation Freemason, and this year I have the great honor of being appointed as
the Grand Orator.
Seven generations! My family has seen Freemasonry evolve from what it
was then to what it is now.
Seven generations! My family has seen Freemasonry survive devastating
wars and terrorist attacks.
Seven generations! My family has seen Freemasonry withstand the effects
of terrible pandemics.
Seven generations! My family has seen Freemasonry stay true to its traditions and beliefs.
We have come so far as a fraternity. For seven generations, my family has
seen what an impact Freemasonry has left in this world and in our society. But I
believe our job as a Fraternity is far from finished. Lately, I am noticing a breakdown in society, where simple arguments turn violent, and where a different
opinion is no longer respected. I believe that as members of this fraternity, we
can and should help.
If we don’t help, then who?
If we don’t act now, then when?
If we don’t start here, right here, then where?
For those of you who don’t know what the job of a Grand Orator is, let me
explain. One of the most important parts of being a Grand Orator is to prepare
and deliver an address to the brethren of California on the state and vision of
the Fraternity. Maybe even accepting a little guidance from the Grand Master.

138

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

I suppose that would only be proper given that I was appointed by him. Our
Grand Master’s theme this year is “Embracing the Next Evolution.” Throughout
this year, I’ve heard our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Art Wiess, speak about
the 2025 Plan leading into the 2050 vision—“The World in Harmony.”
I would like to see a show of hands. How many brethren in this room can
name the three pillars of the 2025 Plan? It is my hope that at the end of this
oration, I will have accomplished two things: For everyone in this room to
understand the importance of the 2025 Plan and to help accomplish it; and for
you to not devise your own plan on how to escape this oration.
The three pillars of the Fraternity’s 2025 Plan are:
1. True Friendship
2. Diversity and Harmony
3. Positive Awareness
True friendship, in my opinion, is the easiest one to accomplish. Every single
person, from our most senior Past Grand Master to our newest Master Mason,
wouldn’t be sitting in this room had there not been a friend who believed in
you. Believed that you had more to offer. Believed that society needed you to
step up and make this world a better place. Everyone remembers the person
who gave them their application. That was a true friend. Someone who thought
Masonry would be at a disadvantage without you. I can stand here and say, I
know a majority of you in here, and I believe that, too.
Let me see another show of hands. Raise your hand if you’ve made most of
your true friends through Masonry. Is David Vassall in the room? David, would
you please stand up? Everyone, I would like for you to meet David Vassall,
master of San Diego No. 35. David, would you have ever imagined having so
many brothers?
David is one of my best friends, and our friendship began many years ago
in lodge. He proposed to his wife Amanda here in San Francisco during Annual
Communication in 2018, and they got married this past June. The reason I am
telling you this is that he asked me to be one of his groomsmen in his wedding.
It gets better. My wife, Kasey, was a bridesmaid, my daughter, Idy, was the flower
girl, and my son, Michael, the ring bearer. Our entire family was in their wedding.
One of the most important decisions and one of the most sacred ceremonies
of David’s life, he wanted my entire family to take part. That’s true friendship,
and all because of this wonderful Fraternity.
Freemasonry is what helps us develop the strong bonds of friendship we
have. I don’t go to lodge for the food or to hear the minutes read of the previous
meeting. I go because that’s where my true friends are.
Along with the application you received, everyone also probably remembers
that first time they showed up to a lodge function. You didn’t know anybody,
you were out of your element, and that can be extremely daunting. This, for the
lodge, can be the golden hour. If you make them feel accepted and welcomed,
they’ll come back. On the other hand, if you don’t, chances are you will never

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

139

see that applicant again.
I challenge everyone in this room that when you return home, to call two
of your newest members and make them feel welcome. Ask them about their
family, and tell them about yours. How about inviting them to a lodge function
or meeting them for coffee. Whatever it is you choose to do, let them feel for
themselves the true friendship that Freemasonry is known for.
I believe in you. Freemasonry believes in you. Do you believe in you?
The second pillar: Diversity and Harmony. I was in the Navy for five years,
did three deployments and visited many countries. But I will always remember
the first time I went to Hong Kong with my wife. Talk about nervous. I wasn’t
there on vacation. I was there to get to know the family and culture that I had
just married into. New customs, new food, a new way of life—even the air felt
different. But my excitement to meet my new family outweighed the fear I had
being halfway across the world and out of my comfort zone. Truthfully, it took
a few visits for me to truly appreciate the customs and the traditions. I’m so
thankful that I was able to step outside my safe place and immerse myself in
this new culture. Now Hong Kong feels like a home away from home.
My first experience going to Hong Kong is similar to some situations we
find ourselves in Freemasonry. No one likes to be outside their comfort zone.
We are naturally drawn to things we are familiar with. We like to hang out
with people who have the same interests, the same mindset, or speak the same
language. It’s easy—we feel more at ease. As a result, we unintentionally form
little social circles.
Although it is important for us to step outside our safe space so we don’t
form these cliques, it is equally important for us to put ourselves out there and
try to immerse ourselves in these different groups. The next time you go to
the lodge, instead of making a beeline to the group of friends you are familiar
with, go introduce yourself to a different crowd. Ask them questions. Ask them
what they are talking about. What about bringing one of your friends along and
introducing them to this new group as well? Together we can make our lodges
a home away from home for all Masons.
I believe you can. Freemasonry believes you can. Do you believe you can?
The last pillar is a piece of cake!
For the last time, a show of hands: How many of you in this room are proud
to call yourself a Mason? Are proud of what Freemasonry is accomplishing in the
state of California? Are proud of the friendships you’ve made? If you answered
yes to any or all of these questions, it becomes your obligation to not let this
Fraternity become the best thing people don’t know about. Get out, talk about
Freemasonry and the good that it does for our society. Tell people how much
Freemasonry means to you, and let them know how much this world needs it.
I believe you should. Freemasonry believes you should. Do you believe
you should?
A world in harmony by 2050. Wouldn’t that be nice? Will we be able to
achieve what our mission statement says, “Building peace and understanding

140

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

through friendship, service, and self-improvement?” Absolutely! I believe we
can. If we can all come together and put our best foot forward and accomplish
all of the pillars that were laid out in the 2025 Plan—True Friendship, Diversity
and Harmony, and Positive Awareness—I believe we will see results. We will
be one step closer to the next evolution, “The World in Harmony.” Can you
imagine the world we would live in? Can you imagine being able to express your
opinion freely without judgement or fear of repercussion? Can you imagine
everyone living in harmony? For that, we can, we should, and we will act now
and start here.
Freemasonry believes in us. The world believes in us, and we should most
definitely believe in ourselves.
Thank you and God bless you.
Respectfully submitted,
Michael D. Thibodeaux, Grand Orator

2021 GRAND LODGE LEGISLATION
GRAND MASTER’S DECISIONS
AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 1
Ratification Of Actions
at the 171st Annual Communication
The COVID-19 pandemic and the restrictions imposed by the State of
California to address the pandemic required this Grand Lodge to conduct its
171st Annual Communication virtually. Grand Master Trauner’s Decision No.
2 to hold the 171st Annual Communication virtually was legal and within his
discretion. Yet, it would be prudent and best for our historical record for this
Grand Lodge at its immediately subsequent Annual Communication to ratify
and affirm the unprecedented but necessary actions taken last year to conduct
its business.
If you adopt this recommendation, all actions taken at the 171st Annual
Communication will be ratified, including the Installation of Grand Lodge
Officers, and Most Worshipful Brother John E. Trauner’s status as a Past Grand
Master will be affirmed.

144

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 2
Establishes the Lodge Executive Committee
as a Standing Committee
Our members tell us they are looking for more meaningful lodge experiences,
including more efficient and more engaging Stated Meetings. Many Lodges are
now using an executive committee to plan lodge meetings and ensure that the
Lodge is operating in an efficient and successful manner. The executive committee consists of the Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary. Lodges with
executive committees have shown good progress in providing well planned
meetings and meaningful engagement for their members.
This recommendation provides a framework for all Lodges to benefit from
this best practice. This resolution does not, however, change the authority of
the Lodge to act and decide on matters before the Lodge as they do presently.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 806.000 of the Code will be
amended as marked:
§806.000. COMMITTEES.
A.

The Master and Wardens shall be a Charity Committee, and shall
have the power to draw upon the funds of the Lodge for any sum,
not exceeding $100 at any one time (or such greater amount as the
Lodge may from time to time provide by a standing resolution), for
the relief of a distressed worthy Mason and the wife, widow or orphan
of a Master Mason.

B.

The Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary shall be an Executive
Committee, and shall meet at some time prior to each Stated Meeting,
at a time and place and in a manner designated by the Master who
shall chair the Committee. Its duties shall be to assist the Master
concerning the operation and affairs of the Lodge and to perform
such other duties as he may designate.

CB. The Master, at the Stated Meeting next succeeding his installation,
shall appoint an Auditing Committee, whose duty it shall be to
examine all accounts presented against the Lodge and the books
and records of the Treasurer and Secretary. Neither the Treasurer
nor Secretary may serve on the Audit Committee.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

145

DC. The Master, at the Stated Meeting next succeeding his installation,
shall appoint a Member Retention Committee to personally, or otherwise, interview each delinquent Mason, ascertain the cause, and
work closely with the Master and officers in a continuing effort to
effect the retention of all worthy brothers unable to pay.
ED. The Lodge may have such other committees as the Master or the
Lodge may deem proper to appoint. All committees shall be appointed
by the Master, unless the Lodge provides otherwise.
FE. All reports of committees shall be in writing.
GF. Only members of the Lodge in good standing may serve on a Lodge’s
committees.

146

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 3
Permits Virtual Participation in Stated Meetings
At the 171st Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge, Sections
807.000 and 807.010 of the California Masonic Code were amended to allow
for entirely virtual Stated Meetings when assembling the required number of
persons for holding a Stated or Special Meeting is prohibited by government
authority. These amendments allowed our Lodges to continue to transact
important business during the COVID-19 Pandemic. With the withdrawal of
government prohibitions on private meeting and events, Lodges may now meet
in person. I hope we never again have cause to rely upon these amendments.
During the pandemic, however, we learned that virtual participation at
Stated Meetings provided opportunities for certain Masons to participate in
Lodge who in the past had been unable to do so or who could only do so infrequently or with difficulty.
This recommendation provides a path for Masons to continue to participate in their Lodge in-person Stated Meetings. This recommendation would
permit, but not require, Lodges to provide opportunities for their members,
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts to attend virtually the business portion
of in-person Stated Meetings.
This recommendation does not permit Lodges to hold entirely virtual
Stated Meetings. A Lodge may do so only if the conditions and requirements
of Section 807.000 for an entirely virtual Stated Meeting are met.
In preparing this recommendation, I have considered a number of factors
from our brethren concerning modes of recognition and other ritualistic matters,
balloting, and the participation of officers and other Masons.
Regarding modes of recognition, which is to say the due guards and signs
a Mason displays when addressing the Master of the Lodge, a concern was that
someone other than the Mason may inadvertently view the modes of recognition
displayed during the business portion of a Stated Meeting. To address this, my
recommendation directs that the Lodge room camera be focused exclusively on
the Master, who does not return any modes of recognition when he is addressed.
As such, no inadvertent communication of the secrets of Masonry could be
revealed to a non-Mason in this manner. Other ritualistic participation, including
the conferral of degrees or examination of candidates, which include recitation
of oral sections of the ritual, as well as displays of the methods of recognition,
are not included as permitted activities for virtual participation. Within this
recommendation we have limited the participation to specific portions of the

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

147

Order of Business, which begins with the reading of the minutes, which occurs
after the ritual for opening the stated meeting, and ends with the completion of
miscellaneous and unfinished business, which immediately precedes conferral
of degrees and also the ritual for the closing of the Lodge. In the same vein of
thinking, no participation in virtual special meetings are included in the recommendation, as those meetings are intended for brief business subjects and
predominantly deal with the conferral of degrees and ceremonies.
Balloting is an important aspect of a lodge’s business, as well as the election
of an applicant to receive degrees or affiliate. As with previous virtual stated
meetings, this recommendation extends the ability for members to participate
in voice votes as a Lodge where the Master judges the outcome of the vote by
listening to the members vocalize their intent. In other ballots, such as balloting
upon applications using the ballot box, or other secret ballots, members participating virtually would be unable to participate in those votes. This is consistent
with the directions I provided with my directive on virtual stated meetings in
November of 2020. For these reasons, members participating virtually would
not be counted in the quorum of a lodge.
The Officers of the Lodge are essential to the business of the Lodge, and
therefore must be present when the Lodge is at labor. For that reason, all officers
of the lodge must be present. They may not participate in their officer position
remotely. That is to say, if the Mason who is the installed Senior Deacon of a
Lodge is unable to be present in person, the person who is occupying the chair
of the Senior Deacon in the Lodge room is the Senior Deacon of the Lodge at
that moment. This does not bar the Mason who is an installed officer from
participating in the stated meeting virtually.
I have left it to the discretion of the Lodge as how to best engage its Masons
virtually. The only requirement written into my recommendation is that the
Lodge room camera be placed on the Master, and not elsewhere in the Lodge.
This could be accomplished by a laptop on the Master’s podium or other means.
It would be permissible for the Lodge to display its remote Masons to those
in the Lodge room.
These are important matters to consider when continuing the virtual participation of Masons in our Stated Meetings.
If you adopt this recommendation, a new Section 807.005 would be added
to the Code to read as follows:
§807.005. LIMITED VIRTUAL STATED MEETING PARTICIPATION.
The Master of a Lodge may authorize the Lodge to allow its Masons to
participate in the business portion of a Stated Meeting virtually through
the use of conference telephone, electronic video communication or electronic transmission, provided that all of the following conditions are met:
A. Virtual attendance by a Mason of the Lodge at a Stated Meeting is
permitted only during the following portions of business as defined

148

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

in Section 807.030 of this Code:
1.

Reading of the minutes;

2.

Reports of investigating committees;

3.

Balloting;

4.

Reception of applications; and

5.

Miscellaneous and unfinished business.

B. During the portions of the Stated Meeting that a Mason of the Lodge
may attend virtually:
1.

Each Mason participating virtually in the meeting can communicate with all of the other Masons concurrently and is provided
the means of participating in the meeting, when recognized by
the Master.

2.

Each member participating virtually is permitted to vote on matters before the Lodge arising during the portion of the meeting
where virtual attendance is permitted, provided that the vote is
taken by voice vote, by hand or by rising vote. Members participating virtually shall not participate in any vote taken by ballot
and shall not be considered present for the purposes of any vote
by ballot.

3.

Video transmission, if any, to Masons participating virtually is
limited to video of the Master. Video transmission of Masons of
the Lodge participating virtually, if any, is at the discretion of the
Master.

C. No Mason participating virtually may fill an officer place or station.
D. A member participating virtually is not counted in attendance for
purposes of determining a quorum.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Grand Master Weiss’s Recommendation No. 4
Negotiated Settlement at Mediation to be Binding and Final
Mediation has become an effective tool for this Grand Lodge to settle
disputes among brothers and reduce the number of Masonic Trials for unmasonic conduct. This Grand Lodge formalized the process into the California
Masonic Code with its adoption of Grand Master Wright’s Recommendation
No. 4 at the 170th Annual Communication.
However, an accused brother may be reluctant to enter into a negotiated
settlement made during a mediation if he believes someone other than the
known accusers will bring charges on the same subject at a later date. It is in
this Grand Lodge’s interest that disputes among brothers be settled with finality.
A brother who has agreed to a mediated settlement should not be subject to
charges on the same subject matter at a later date. In my view, this result would
be unfair and a form of double jeopardy.
If you adopt this recommendation, the Code would be amended to permit
the negotiated settlement at the mediation of a charge of unmasonic conduct
to become the binding and final resolution of the matter. To protect against
potential abuse, the negotiated settlement would be a binding and final resolution of the matter only if after review it is so ordered by the Grand Master
with the concurrence of the Committee on Trial Review
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to the
Code. Section 1404.570 of the Code which would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.570. DISMISSAL.
If in the Trial Master’s judgment all of the evidence introduced at trial,
taken together, would not warrant a guilty verdict on a charge of unmasonic
conduct, then he shall dismiss such charge. The trial record shall set forth
the dismissal and the Trial Master’s reasons for it. Subject to the provisions
of Section 1404.950 of the Code, sSuch a dismissal shall not prevent any
subsequent filing of the same or similar charge but with more evidence.
The Trial Master shall notify the Grand Secretary of such dismissal
and the reasons for it. The Grand Secretary shall then notify the Accuser
and the Accused of the action taken, as well as the Accused’s Lodge and
the Inspector assigned to such Lodge. If the Accused is a member of more
than one Lodge, the notification shall be given to every Lodge of which the
Accused is a member, as shown in Grand Lodge’s records, and the Inspector

150

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

assigned to each such Lodge.
Section 1404.950 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.950. DOUBLE JEOPARDY.
When Grand Lodge determines that the Accused ought not to have been
convicted, and sets aside a verdict of conviction without ordering a new
trial, its judgment is final, and the Accused may not be tried again on the
same charge.
Upon Grand Lodge’s review and approval, a conviction or acquittal
on a charge of unmasonic conduct under this Code is a bar to a future
prosecution on the same charge in this Jurisdiction.
If so ordered by the Grand Master with the concurrence of the
Committee on Trial Review, a dismissal of a charge of unmasonic conduct
under this Code is a bar to a future prosecution on the same charge in this
Jurisdiction.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a
