REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
California Masonic Foundation
Despite the hardship of the COVID-19 crisis, the California Masonic
Foundation, led by its chairman, John R. Heisner, and its president, Doug Ismail,
has continued to fulfill its mission to provide relief to those with the greatest
need and improve our communities.
In 2021, California Masons donated more than $1.5 million to the Foundation
to support its charitable programs—all the more impressive given that, for most
of the year, Masons were unable to meet in person and visits from Foundation
staff were put on hold. That the giving spirit remains so strong during this
difficult time is evidence of our membership’s commitment to the principles
of Freemasonry.
A highlight of 2021 has of course been the continued success of the Distressed
Worthy Brother Relief Fund. Launched in spring 2020, the fund has raised more
than $1.13 million for Masons and their families who have been affected by the
pandemic. In 2021, the program was incorporated into the Foundation’s Annual
Fund and expanded to support the Masonic Homes of California’s commitment
to Masonic relief. This fund will anchor the Foundation’s ongoing efforts to
ensure that the most vulnerable members of the Fraternity, as well as their
families and widows, are provided for and remain safe and healthy.
Elsewhere, the Foundation in 2021 continued to support its long-running
charitable programs. Donations to Masons4Mitts, now in its 13th year, are up
significantly compared with 2020, though still well below previous years’ levels.
As COVID-19 restrictions loosened, the program began to rebound, with captain’s nights held at the end of July in all four regions, and Masons Night at the
Ballpark events taking place in late September.
The Foundation has also continued its long-standing support for public
education and children’s literacy. Since 2011, the Foundation has partnered with
the national nonprofit Raising A Reader, which provides under-resourced public
schools and students with expert-vetted, age-appropriate books, encouraging
families to foster a love of reading. Since the launch of that partnership, the
Foundation has donated more than $3.5 million to Raising A Reader—including
$422,000 in 2020–21—helping the program expand to 717 classrooms across
180 of the lowest-performing schools statewide.
In addition to Raising A Reader, the Foundation is committed to providing
support to high school graduates through four different scholarship programs:

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

215

the CE Towne Masonic Scholarship, given in partnership with Prince Hall
Masons; the Masonic Youth Leadership Award; the Investment in Success
scholarship program; and a new pilot, the Working Tools scholarship. COVID-19
has presented difficulty in particular for these programs, as many students and
families have faced tremendous uncertainty over their college plans. Distance
learning has also impacted students’ performance, and as a result, Foundation
staff worked harder than ever to identify and distribute these signature awards
to deserving students.
Despite those hurdles, it was a successful year for the Foundation’s college-assistance programs: In 2021, the CE Towne Masonic Scholarship had the
largest distribution in its history, with more than $150,000 given to 23 students.
Similarly, the Masonic Youth Leadership scholarship distributed nearly $185,000
to 34 individuals, the program’s largest distribution to date. Additionally, the
Investment in Success program was able to issue scholarships to 64 deserving
young people, exceeded the goal established in 2020. A pilot program, the
Working Tools scholarship, was also launched with the aim of supporting high
school graduates pursuing a career in the trades. The program gives tuition
assistance to qualified high school graduates attending trade school or vocational
programs—and represents the Foundation’s belief that four-year college isn’t
a student’s only path to a rewarding career. The pandemic has certainly complicated the rollout of the Working Tools scholarship, limiting the number of
applications. However, as schools resume in-person instruction, the Foundation
anticipates significant growth for the program.
The year 2021 saw the California Masonic Foundation shift its near-term
fundraising focus away from the Let’s Write the Future campaign and toward
an expansion of the Cornerstone Society, which recognizes donors who provide
for the Foundation in their will or estate plan. The campaign was launched in
spring 2021 and will conclude in 2025, the 175th anniversary of the Grand Lodge
of California. Planned giving is a crucial aspect of the fraternity’s operations,
and represents the charitable foundation on which the organization is built.
The board would like to thank and congratulate Most Worshipful Arthur
H. Weiss for his leadership this past year. With the launch of the fraternity’s
2025 Strategic Plan, the Foundation is prepared to do its part in making the
plan a success. The California Masonic Foundation is working diligently to
ensure its charitable programs are well funded, well utilized, and efficiently
run—improving the lives of those around us.
Respectfully submitted,

Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Treasurer
Allan L. Casalou, Secretary

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
The California Masonic Memorial Temple
Although the halls and offices of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple (CMMT) have been uncharacteristically quiet this past year and a half,
there has nevertheless been plenty of activity behind the scenes as we’ve worked
to ensure a rapid recovery. And with the first of 30 planned concerts and shows
taking the Masonic stage on August 23, the volume is picking up.
In previous years, some 200,000-plus visitors have come through the doors
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple. But with Live Nation being dark
for 17 months, that number dropped precipitously in 2021. However, things are
turning a corner. With the resumption of concerts and special events inside the
Masonic auditorium, plus the return to work in August of much of the third-floor
office staff and preparations for an in-person Annual Communication in October,
a familiar buzz is returning to the 63-year-old temple. That bodes well for the
financial outlook of the California Masonic Memorial Temple moving forward.
In lieu of in-person events at the CMMT in 2021, the most visible activity
inside the building related to ongoing facilities upgrades. The 10-year capital
improvements plan approved by the board in 2019 was most recently updated
in August to account for labor and materials shortages and delays. Overall,
though, forecasts for the Capital Plan have improved for fiscal year 2021 due to
overall lower costs, contributions from Live Nation, and better overall financial
performance. Among the projects completed in fiscal year 2021 were electrical
panel testing and roof resurfacing. Several other projects are ongoing, including
replacement of the third-floor air handler; refurbishment of bathrooms, meeting, and eating areas on the third floor; and replacement or repair of the doors
separating the California Street flag porch from the concourse. According to
the plan, all improvements will be paid for through operating cash flow. The
board established a new building improvement reserve fund for these purposes.
These moves—and others, including the redesign of the Grand Lodge
offices and the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum of Freemasonry—are
being made in part with the aim of telling the story of Freemasonry through the
California Masonic Memorial Temple building itself. That priority emerged as a
key element of the 2025 Plan adopted by the CMMT board. As building activity
continues to grow over the course of 2021 and beyond, utilizing the CMMT as
a storytelling asset will become an even larger focus.
Despite the lack of in-person meetings, relations between the CMMT and

218

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

its neighbors remain close, as CMMT holds quarterly meetings through the
Nob Hill Community Liaison Group and neighborhood association meetings
and events. Executive Vice President and Secretary Allan Casalou continues
to serve as a director of the Nob Hill Association and on the Huntington Park
Committee, which is chaired by Khalil Sweidy, a Nob Hill resident.
In May, the CMMT saw a changing of the guard, with longtime building
and facilities manager Dale Vigil retiring after 23 years of dedicated service to
the Grand Lodge and CMMT. In his place, Jacob Warren was hired to take over
the position. Warren is trained as an electrical technician and comes to CMMT
after 16 years at Expression College, where he rose from facility technician to
director of facilities.
It has been a protracted recovery, but as Lodges have returned to
Freemasons’ Hall, staff to the offices of the third floor, and concertgoers to
the auditorium of the Masonic stage, there is once again light at the end of the
tunnel.
The board wishes to extend its appreciation to Executive Vice President
and Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, Chief Financial Officer Thomas J. Boyer,
Director of Financial Planning and Real Estate Khalil Sweidy, General Counsel
Andy Cameron, and Grand Treasurer Arthur Salazar. Thanks also go to Julia
Gordon for her work in preparing and managing board meetings and materials, as well as building manager Jacob Warren and Joe Evans for his excellent
curation and management of the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum collections. Sincere thanks and appreciation also go out to the staff who work so
diligently in representing the board’s interests and maintaining and managing
the building. Finally, thanks to our grand master, Most Worshipful Arthur Weiss,
for the opportunity to serve, and for his active support of our efforts.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Nob Hill Masonic Center
The past 18 months have represented an unprecedented challenge for most
businesses and organizations. The Nob Hill Masonic Center has been no exception. Practically overnight, many of its core revenue drivers disappeared. As the
shock of the first few weeks of the pandemic gave way to the reality of a slow,
protracted recovery, it became clear that the board of the NHMC needed to
plan for a new reality.
Which is why it is gratifying to report that in 2021, the Nob Hill Masonic
Center has not only stabilized its operations but actually outperformed expectations, and can now look confidently toward a resumption of the growth it
enjoyed pre-pandemic.
As the Grand Lodge of California’s only for-profit entity, the Nob Hill
Masonic Center is responsible for ensuring the efficient and effective operation
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple garage in order to generate an
annual dividend for the Grand Lodge, which is its sole stockholder. Thanks to
aggressive measures put in place early in the pandemic and the formation of a
three-phase recovery plan, as well as reserves generated in previous years, the
NHMC was able to pay a dividend of $390,000 in 2021.
This was the result of enormous changes to the garage’s business model.
Prior to the pandemic and subsequent shutdown orders, daily and special-event
parking represented two of the most important parts of the garage’s revenue
stream. However, with an abrupt decline in both, the NHMC needed to adapt
and find new sources of revenue.
The result was the formation of a three-part recovery plan. Phase one,
implemented in spring 2020, involved aggressive cost-cutting measures to offset
the loss of revenue, as well as the launching of new marketing initiatives aimed
at increasing monthly parking contracts, in addition to pursing opportunities
for expanded fleet and ride-share parking. The second phase, stabilization,
launched in September 2020, saw monthly and daily parking receipts hold steady,
while the garage returned to break-even operations. The NHMC entered the
third and final stage of the plan, rebounding in June 2021 with the growth of
daily revenues, and in late August with the resumption of event revenue as Live
Nation held its first concert inside the California Masonic Memorial Temple in
17 months. (With another 30 planned for the remainder of 2021.)
In all three phases, the NHMC has exceeded expectations, making the

220

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

garage profitable even in the midst of the ongoing pandemic. Monthly parking
agreements not only held steady in 2021 but actually grew compared with 2019,
thanks in large part to online marketing efforts including Google search and
display ads on Facebook and Instagram, Nextdoor, and several parking apps.
(Internet search accounted for close to one-fifth of all new monthly parking
agreements from June to August 2021, up from practically zero prior to that.)
By Q3 of 2021, the NHMC had not only broken even but posted a profit of
$66,000, thanks to its most successful quarter ever in monthly parking revenue.
Installation of a brand-new Parking Access Revenue Control System (or PARCS)
is ongoing and expected to be finished by October.
Growth in the garage’s fleet parking has also been significant, especially
regarding the on-demand rental-car startup Kyte. From June 2020, when the
company leased 30 spaces in the garage, the company expanded to now occupy
85 spaces, with talks ongoing regarding a longer-term agreement.
Growth of both monthly and fleet parking has helped partially offset the
initial loss of daily parking and the total loss of special-event parking for much of
the past year and a half. On balance, the board is able to project fiscal year 2021
being profitable, though still not near pre-pandemic profits. As special events
at the CMMT return in the fall of 2021, the business will continue to evolve
and adapt, with additional spaces needed to accommodate concert parking.
The board is reviewing several possibilities to maximize revenue opportunities.
Profits for the fiscal year ending October 31, 2021 are expected to be approximately $150,000.
The NHMC remains committed to its role as a responsible and engaged
community partner. To that end, board representatives have continued to participate in the neighborhood association, sponsor the annual holiday tree-lighting
ceremony in Huntington Park, and enjoy good relations with their Nob Hill
neighbors.
In 2021, the board also welcomed Kim Nadeau, the parking division manager for the city of Santa Rosa. Her experience with all aspects of parking
management, including overseeing five downtown garages, will be invaluable
to the board.
The pandemic has posed a serious challenge to the operation of the NHMC.
Since March 2020, the fiscal impact of the pandemic to the garage is in excess
of $635,000 in lost net profits. But thanks to the vision and hard work of the
board, the NHMC has not only avoided the worst-case scenario but actually
remained profitable, positioning it for a particularly bright future.
The board wishes to extend its appreciation to its president and chief
executive, Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, and to all the management and staff
of the Grand Lodge who support its business. In addition, it thanks the Grand
Master, Most Worshipful Brother Arthur H. Weiss, and the executive committee
for their confidence and support.

THE GRAND LODGE OF CA
INSURANCE COMMITTEE REPORT 2021
The Masons of California corporate insurance program, which includes
coverage for Lodge, Hall, Masonic Homes, Acacia Creek, and Nob Hill with
property, general liability, umbrella liability, earthquake, D&O, employment,
and crime insurance policies, all renewed April 1, 2021.
We continue as we ended last year’s insurance program, with a tough
renewal. By now we are all aware of the pressures on the insurance industry with
respect to claims payments and losses and the need to increase rates. There is
no relief with deductibles that were implemented three years ago. As you will
see, the insurance program continues to present challenges. In addition to catastrophic losses, insurers have added communicable disease exclusions, which
are being seen across all lines worldwide. The specific exclusion of COVID-19related losses is not unexpected. As was done the past two years, our insurance
broker, Marsh, conducted a full insurance market review. Grand Lodge staff and
the Insurance Committee worked diligently to look at cost-saving areas as well
as ideas beyond traditional insurance transactions. These included self-insurance, insurance captives, and other risk-transfer methods. The committee will
continue to review alternative risk-transfer methods.
During the past 60 months, insurers have incurred significant losses due to
catastrophic fire events in California and elsewhere in the north and southwest,
as we all are aware. As a result, insurers continue to dictate higher premiums
and tighten underwriting and policy terms. Three years ago, moving the halls to
a higher deductible resulted in far fewer losses being reported to the insurer. As
we know, this was a good start; however, we will need several years of reduced
losses, particularly the frequency of losses, if we are to have insurers review this
exposure favorably. Hall programs have experienced higher claims frequencies,
causing insurers to review that part of our program unfavorably.
Marsh reached out early to insurance markets and wholesale brokers. The
result is a 9.3 percent increase on top of a 15 percent increase last year. Marsh
navigated a difficult marketplace, but we are confident that we identified the
most favorable coverages available to us.
Property Insurance Program Renewal
The renewed Hall, Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes, MCYAF, and Acacia Creek
property program includes the following key terms and changes from last year:

• Limits: $5 million (Lloyd’s primary) and $5 million (Lloyd’s excess)
• Limits: Acacia Creek $1 million (Chubb primary), $4 million (Chubb
excess)
• Deductible: $0
• Premium cost: $559,697, an increase of 8 percent over last year
Cyber Liability
These policies are designed to address the ever-growing area of cyber crime,
whether it be internet fraud, phishing scams, identity theft, and hacking. This

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

229

is perhaps the fastest-growing insurance product, and witnessing substantial
premium increases as claims start to be filed.
• Insurers: Coalition and Corvus
• Limits: $5 Million (Coalition primary), $3 million and $2 million
(Corvus Excess)
• Deductible: $25,000
• Premium cost: $30,296, an increase of 37 percent over last year
Workers’ Compensation
The workers’ compensation policies provide the statutory coverage required
to protect employees during the course and scope of their employment. The
workers’ compensation program was marketed three years ago, with Travelers
being the most competitive.
• Insurer: Travelers
• Limits: Statuatory
• Premium: 12 percent increase for deductible program and 8 percent
reduction from last year for the first dollar policy.
• Deductibles: $0 and $250,000 for the large deductible program, same
as expiring
Conclusions
The property program premium increases continue, and we don’t see an end
to that trend as long as there is a 12-month fire season in California. There
is an ongoing drive to increase hall property replacement cost values. This
will help underwriters view us as a stable and well-managed exposure. The
Insurance Committee cannot stress enough that this is not a one-year occurrence. Therefore, hall management should focus on deferred maintenance issues
and start a preventative maintenance program immediately.
The casualty program was moved from Liberty to Travelers three years
ago. Our goal is to continue to try and leverage this into a discussion about the
property program in the future.
Overall, the program was renewed in what continues to be a difficult and
hard market. Insurers are facing huge losses from climate change, fires, hurricanes, and flooding, and these are becoming more frequent and severe. We see no
changes in this trend. Overall, we pushed our broker to persuade underwriters to
provide the best terms possible. In addition, as noted, work must continue with
halls to help them better understand the need to provide realistic replacement

230

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

cost values and understand that good housekeeping directly relates to reduced
premiums. Terrorism coverage is purchased on all the major lines of insurance.
This report would not be complete without recognizing John Lindell, who
has served as Vice Chair and most recently as consultant to the Insurance
Committee. His passing has left a large hole in this committee’s institutional
knowledge, as well as the loss of his deep insurance background. I could not
have succeeded as chair of this committee without his strong support and care
to see that all diligence and help is offered to Grand Lodge staff in providing a
robust and enduring insurance program.

REPORT OF THE
INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent handling of
Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist primarily of the General
and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes of California, but also include
the investment portfolios of the California Masonic Foundation, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, and the Grand Lodge itself.
The financial objectives for these funds we steward are laid out in our
approved Investment Policy Statement:
The primary objectives of the funds are to provide a regular and reliable
source of financial support to the Masonic entity or its beneficiaries, while
preserving the purchasing power of the funds after withdrawals are taken.
In plain English, we are tasked with making sure that the Masonic Homes,
the Foundation, and all entities that are entrusting their funds to our care can
expect to receive a reasonable income, while their principle keeps pace with
expected inflation over time.
As a simple example, if one of the entities wanted to be able to rely on a 4.5
percent distribution from its money, we know we’d have to earn at least that
by investing. If we also expected inflation to be 2 percent per year on average
(eroding purchasing power of the principal), we’d know that we also want to
grow the principal by 2 percent per year on average. We’d then know that we
needed to build a portfolio that could reasonably be expected to return 6.5
percent over the long term (4.5 percent spending plus 2 percent inflation).
This example, while simple, is actually very close to the actual numbers
used to form our return goals for the Grand Lodge investments.
The job of the committee, then, is to build the portfolio with the best
chance of accomplishing that return goal over the long term while exposing
the portfolio to the least risk needed to attain that goal.
While the committee comprises diligent financial professionals who are

232

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

astute in portfolio construction and global economics, we also employ the use
of a robust team of investment consultants that help us quantify and evaluate
the metrics of our portfolio and model the mix of investments that give us the
greatest likelihood of achieving those goals.
Grand Lodge and Related Entity Investment Performance
for the year ending June 30, 2021
The Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio earned a rate of
return of 30.4 percent for the year ending June 30, 2021. The relevant period saw
explosive growth stemming from the prospects of reopening an economy that
had been largely closed down because of the pandemic. The total fund policy
benchmark during the same period was up 27.8 percent. The market value of
the Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio as of June 30, 2021 was
$1,156,031,526. For the three-year period ending June 30, 2021, the combined
Grand Lodge and related entities returned an average return of 11.3 percent
versus 11.5 percent for the benchmark. Since its inception, our funds have
returned 8 percent annually versus the 8.2 percent return of the benchmark.

The Investment Committee has arrived at this investment policy through
a careful study of the returns and risk associated with alternative investment
strategies in relation to the current and projected income needs of each fund.
This policy has been chosen as the most appropriate one for achieving the
financial objectives of the funds.

Year in Review Activity
Allocation Changes:
This year we slightly reduced our exposure to hedge funds and private debt,
and incrementally added to our global equity, emerging markets, and private
equity positions.
I nve s t me nt M ana g e r s H ir ed :
We believe that a disciplined manager-selection process will result in a
higher probability of hiring superior managers. We believe that past performance is an unreliable predictor of future success and is only one of many
factors that should be used in the selection process. During this period, the
managers hired were:
• Private Real Estate/Real Assets: IPI Partners
• Private Equity: Bond Capital, 5Y Capital Evolution, Bain Capital, Mill
Point
• Private Debt: Whitehorse
I nve s t me nt M ana g e r s Ter min at ed :
Once managers have been thoroughly vetted and consistently monitored,
as long as the manager’s investment style is still part of our overall investment
thesis, it is relatively rare that a manager is terminated, unless we have adjusted
the positioning of the portfolio. In the past three years, we have, indeed, made
several positioning changes. Much of the change comes from our positive effort
to create a private markets portion of the portfolio.
As part of our fundamental philosophy, stated in our Investment Policy
Statement:
“We believe that manager turnover is very expensive and extremely
disruptive to the efficient and productive operation of an investment
program. Managers should be hired with a long-run view … We also
believe that constant and/or rapid turnover of managers, justified solely
on the basis of relative underperformance is usually an indication of a
lack of adherence to the selection and retention process. In particular,
short-term (generally less than one year) underperformance should not

234

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

be a reason for termination, unless it is accompanied by other adverse
key retention characteristics.”
During this period, the managers terminated were:
• Hedge Funds: Renaissance Equity
• Opportunistic: Tortoise MLP & Pipeline
Gr a n d L od g e I n v e st men t Manag e me nt
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand Lodge
investment policy and philosophy, the Investment Committee meets quarterly
with our investment consultant NEPC, LLC. We also meet with our individual
portfolio managers as needed and review due diligence reports quarterly from
the consultants. We monitor the respective performance of the managers compared with various indices representing their objective. This process provides
the Investment Committee with the necessary data to evaluate each investment
manager on a timely basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve
the objectives of their mandate.
The committee also holds ad hoc conference calls to discuss any outstanding business or discuss the implementation of tactical changes within
the portfolio.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist individual Lodges in determining appropriate investment strategies. We are also here
to help Lodges establish a set of policies and procedures that are designed to
ensure assets are invested according to the needs of the Lodge and to safeguard
against the misuse of funds. Investment Committee members continue to make
themselves available to the Lodges for assistance with this program and other
questions regarding Lodge investments.
S u mma r y
I am honored to present this report on behalf of the Investment Committee
of the Grand Lodge of California. They continue to work with zeal to ensure
that your assets are properly stewarded, and I am glad to have their efforts and
dedication. I want to thank Syd Walker for his tremendous service to the Craft
and the committee during his tenure. Thank you for allowing me to serve as
chair this year; it is both an honor and a privilege to work with all the gentlemen
on the Committee.
I want to thank Julia Gordon for her tireless work supporting all our committees, and Very Worshipful Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Tom Boyer, and Linh Pham,
who manage the day-to-day flows and intricacies of the assets of our related
entities. Thank you.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON JURISPRUDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the Grand Master
and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the
next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.

Grand Master Weiss’s
Decisions and Dispensations
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Weiss’s decisions and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
At the beginning of his term, Grand Master Weiss decided to continue Grand
Master Trauner’s March 18, 2020 decision on Masonic Events During COVID-19
and Grand Master Trauner’s May 6, 2020 decision on Dues Remissions During
COVID-19 (as set forth in the 2020 Report of the Committee on Jurisprudence).
The committee’s views on these decisions, finding them legal and within Grand
Master Trauner’s discretion, can be found in its report for the 171st Annual
Communication.
Grand Master Weiss’s Decision No. 1:
Virtual Stated and Special Meetings
On October 19, 2020, Grand Master Weiss issued a decision entitled “Virtual
Stated and Special Meetings,” in which he determined that assembling the
required number of persons for holding a Stated or Special Meeting was prohibited by competent local, state, or national authority, and then implemented
the virtual meeting provisions of CMC §§807.000 and 807.010 (as is more fully

246

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

set in Exhibit A attached). In the Committee’s view, this decision was legal and
within the Grand Master Weiss’s discretion.
Grand Master Weiss’s Decision No. 2: Restrictions on Masonic-Sponsored
Meetings and Events During COVID-19
On October 19, 2020, Grand Master Weiss issued a decision entitled
“Restrictions on Masonic-Sponsored Meetings and Events During COVID-19”
to address the California Department of Public Health’s October 9 guidance
permitting limited, outdoor social gatherings of no more than three households
for durations of under two hours (as is more fully set in Exhibit B, attached). The
Grand Master noted that the department’s October 9 guidance still effectively
prohibited Masonic-sponsored meetings and events; accordingly, he directed
that there be no in-person Masonic-sponsored meetings or events of any kind
until further directed by him. His decision included Masonic organizations and
Masonic youth orders. His decision also provided limited exceptions for Masonic
funerals and burial services and for the attendance of events not sponsored by
a lodge, hall, Masonic organization, or youth order.
The Grand Master amended his October 2020 decision by way of two
directives to permit in-person meetings and events. The first of these reopening
directives, issued on April 13, 2021 and effective as of April 15, 2021, permitted
in-person meetings and events subject to certain limitations (as is more fully
set in Exhibit C, attached). The Grand Master’s April 13 directive was made with
reference to the State of California’s “COVID-19 Blueprint for a Safer Economy”
(also known as the state’s reopening plan), and the limitations set forth in the
directive were made to ensure compliance with the state’s reopening plan as
well as the orders and guidance of local counties. Those limitations included risk
assessment using available CDC, state, and county guidance and the creation
and adherence to site-specific COVID-19 prevention plans by halls and lodges.
The second of the reopening directives, issued by the Grand Master on June 2,
2021 and effective on June 15, 2021, was based on the California Department of
Health’s decision to lift all of its restrictions on in-person meetings excluding
those that exceed 5,000 people (as is more fully set in Exhibit D, attached). The
Grand Master’s June 2 directive superseded his April 13 directive and permitted
Masonic Lodges, Masonic organizations, and youth orders to hold in-person
meetings and events provided that those meetings and events complied with
county and city restrictions as well as state and county guidance on face coverings. It also allowed Lodges to continue to hold virtual Stated Meetings at
their discretion.
As our committee noted last year, during intervals between Annual
Communications of Grand Lodge, the Grand Master may exercise all executive
powers of the Grand Lodge (CMC §404.120.A), and in the committee’s view,
the executive power of the Grand Lodge includes the power to take reasonable
action proportional to the circumstances to protect lodges and lodge members
during an emergency. Additionally, the Grand Master’s directives were made to
ensure lodges comply with restrictions imposed by competent state authority.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

247

Accordingly, it is the committee’s view that Grand Master Weiss’s Decision No.
2 was legal and within his legal discretion.
Proposed Recommendations and Resolutions
In the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on July 30 of this year is sufficient to carry out the intent
of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master Weiss’s recommendations, which he will present in his message, is sufficient to carry out
his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set
forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no recommendations as to the action to be taken with it. While the committee has written the
title and introductory explanation for each resolution before you and assisted
the proponents in drafting the Code changes required to effect their intent, the
proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own. The committee
does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge website
on July 30 of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Weiss’s
recommendations require no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires only
a simple majority for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code
or the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it
carries over to the next Annual Communication, whereupon only a two-thirds
affirmative vote is required for adoption.
Committee Actions on Unmasonic Conduct
In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews all charges
and specifications of unmasonic conduct, strikes out those portions that are
not supported by a clear and precise specification of unmasonic conduct, and
revises those portions which are incorrect, ambiguous, or insufficient. As part
of its review, the committee provides the parties with every essential factual
element that must be proven at trial for the Accused to be found guilty of each
charge. The Committee may dismiss charges if all the facts set forth in the
specifications, even if true, would not warrant a verdict of unmasonic conduct.
If in the committee’s judgment a dispute warrants pretrial mediation, the Grand
Master may at his discretion appoint one or more Master Masons to mediate
any such dispute. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee commented on the charges and specifications in six trials.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge has
pleaded guilty or nolo contendere (no contest) to, or has been convicted of, a

248

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he shall be deemed automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry without any
further action of his Lodge or Grand Lodge. The committee reviews a certified
copy of the record of conviction to determine whether there has been an automatic expulsion. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee has
reviewed three federal or state court records to evaluate whether there has
been an automatic expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These
matters are summarized in the attached Exhibit E.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any Constituent
Lodge who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of, a
crime involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that he did
not commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of
conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to background checks
to determine compliance with this rule. Since the last Annual Communication,
the Grand Secretary has asked the committee to review no federal or state court
records to evaluate whether an applicant is eligible for the degrees.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity he has given us to serve
this year.

Automatic Expulsions
October 12, 2020 to October 7, 2021
Trial No. 2790
In Trial No. 2709, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal
Code Section 503. This Section provides that “[e]mbezzlement is the fraudulent

250

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

appropriation of property by a person to whom it is [e]ntrusted.” Under Section
100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No.
2, embezzlement involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the
conduct described in California Penal Code Section 503 involves embezzlement. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing analysis, it is the
judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence
that the member pled guilty to a crime of moral turpitude before a state court.
Accordingly, the member was automatically expelled from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic
Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective on March 20, 2020, the date
he entered his plea of guilty.
Trial No. 2791
In Trial No. 2791, the member was convicted of a violation of California
Penal Code Section 647(a). This Section provides that any person who solicits
anyone to engage in or who engages in lewd or dissolute conduct in any public
place or in any place open to the public or exposed to public view is guilty of a
misdemeanor. Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009
Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, lewdness involves moral turpitude. In the
committee’s opinion, the conduct described in California Penal Code Section
647(a) involves lewdness. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing
analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on
Jurisprudence that the member was convicted of a crime of moral turpitude
before a state court. Accordingly, the member was automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the
California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective on March
12, 2020, the date of his conviction.
Trial No. 2797
In Trial No. 2797, the member pled no contest to violations of California
Health and Safety Code Section 11352(a); California Health and Safety Code
Section 11351; California Health and Safety Code Section 11378; and California
Health and Safety Code Section 11359(b). California Health and Safety Code
Section 11352(a) provides that every person who transports for sale any [cocaine],
except as provided by law, shall be punished by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code. California Health and Safety
Code Section 11351 provides that every person who possesses for sale of any
[cocaine], except as provided by law, shall by punished by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code. California Health and
Safety Code Section 11378 provides that every person who possesses for sale of
any [MDMA], shall be punished by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h)
of Section 1170 of the Penal Code. California Health and Safety Code Section
11359(b) provides that every person who possesses for sale of any [marijuana],
except as provided by law, shall be punished by imprisonment pursuant to

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

251

subdivision (h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code. Under 2009 Grand Master’s
Decision No. 2, trafficking in any controlled substance involves moral turpitude
for purposes of Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code. This decision does
not define the term trafficking. However, under California Health and Safety
Code Section 11380.7(d)(4), the term “trafficking” means any of the unlawful
activities specified in California Health and Safety Code Sections 11351, 11351.5,
11352, 11353, 11354, 11378, 11379, 11379.6, and 11380. These provisions define
drug trafficking broadly to include the illegal production and distribution of
controlled substances. The U.S. Supreme Court has similarly concluded under
federal law that trafficking must involve “some sort of commercial dealing.”
See Lopez v. Gonzales, 127 S. Ct. 625, 630 (2006). While 2009 Grand Master’s
Decision No. 2 does not define the term “controlled substance,” the Drug
Enforcement Agency (DEA) of the U. S. Department of Justice publishes a list of
controlled substances. In the list published on September 6, 2012, a controlled
substance includes cocaine, MDMA, and marijuana. Under Section 100.075 of
the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, trafficking
involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in
California Health and Safety Code Sections 11352, 11351, 11378, and 11359 involves
trafficking. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing analysis, it is
the judgment of a majority of the members of the Committee on Jurisprudence
that the member pled no contest to a crime of moral turpitude before a state
court. Accordingly, the member was automatically expelled from all the rights
and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic
Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective on November 29, 2018, the date
he entered his plea of no contest.

GRAND MASTER’S RECOMMENDATIONS

Recommendation No. 1
This recommendation seeks to ratify the actions that took place during the 171st
Annual Communication, including the installation of Grand Lodge Officers and
Most Worshipful John Trauner’s status as a Past Grand Master.
Most Worshipful Trauner’s Decision No. 2 allowed the 171st Annual
Communication to be held virtually. Grand Lodge convened and its work
included, but was not limited to, financial matters and the election of the 2020
Grand Lodge Officers. That election was done virtually.
A similar issue arose in 1945, when this Grand Lodge was unable to meet
due to government-imposed travel restrictions related to World War II. In 1946,
this Grand Lodge adopted a resolution similar to this one to ratify decisions
and actions taken in 1945.
The actions and decisions taken at the 171st Annual Communication were
legal. The acceptance of this recommendation would not have any impact or
require any changes to the California Masonic Code. This resolution is a precautionary measure. But the adoption of this recommendation would create a clear
historical record and remove any basis to challenge the actions taken during
the last Annual Communication, as a similar measure did in 1946.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek

Recommendation No. 2
This recommendation would require each Lodge to have an Executive
Committee. That committee would be composed of the Master, Wardens,
Treasurer, and Secretary of the Lodge. And it would be required to meet some
time prior to every Stated Meeting.
This recommendation would amend California Masonic Code, section 806.000
to add the Executive Committee to the list of standing committees that each
Lodge is required to have. CMC section 806.000 governs Lodge committees and
it currently requires only three standing committees: the Charity Committee, the
Auditing Committee, and the Member Retention Committee. It also authorizes
the Lodge or Master to form any other committee they deem proper.
Protecting Lodge autonomy has been important to this Grand Lodge since
its formation. Some practices are beneficial for some Lodges and not others.
Mandating practices has typically arisen from legal requirements or a compelling reason. While there is no legal reason for requiring every Lodge to have an
Executive Committee, there may be a compelling one.
The benefits of Executive Committees are well established. The Lodge
Manual explains how the Grand Lodge Executive Committee works, and then
explains how a Lodge could and should create its own Executive Committee
to help build a consistent vision and sustained leadership for a Lodge over a
multi-year period. The Lodge Health Check, a resource published by the Grand
Lodge, mentions “Executive Committee” 32 times while touting the benefits
and uses for such a committee. And a “Cohesive Executive Committee” is the
first characteristic of “Strong Lodges and Halls” identified in the Long-Term
Planning Guide.
By contrast, mandating Executive Committees should create a minimal
burden for those Lodges that do not already have them. CMC section 805.210
already requires Wardens to “assist the Master in the performance of his duties.”
And the duties of Secretaries and Treasurers—as specified in CMC sections
805.220 and 805.230—already require them to work with each other and the
Master.
The burdens of an Executive Committee are typically minimal. It is likely
that most members already expect the elected officers of their Lodge to meet
regularly. And the meetings need not be in person; they can be done virtually
or over the phone.
It is for this voting body to decide whether the benefits of requiring every
Lodge to have an Executive Committee outweigh the burdens and the resulting

254

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

infringement on Lodge autonomy.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek
David Doan
Peter Ackeret, Chairman

Recommendation No. 3
This recommendation seeks to give a Lodge the option to make the business
portion of its Stated Meetings available for virtual participation.
Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it became necessary to find ways for Lodges
throughout the state to stay connected to their members and to conduct business. Virtual meetings through the use of Zoom and similar technologies became
the standard for business meetings throughout the nation. Lodges started using
virtual meetings to assemble together for social events even before their use
was authorized for Stated Meetings.
During the past year, Lodges have held virtual Stated Meetings. The procedures and limited scope of those meetings protected the confidentiality of
sensitive matters. As Lodges are returning to in-person meetings, some have
expressed interest in maintaining the newfound accessibility that virtual meeting have provided.
This recommendation would authorize a hybrid of a traditional in-person
Stated Meeting and a virtual meeting. In the Lodge room, the brethren physically
present would be giving the Due Guard and Sign of the First Degree throughout the meeting. Since it is impossible to effectively tile a virtual meeting, this
recommendation would require the camera only be turned on during reading
of the minutes, reports of investigating committees, balloting, reception of
applications, and miscellaneous and unfinished business. Further, the camera
would be solely focused on the Master, who never gives the Due Guard or Sign
during these portions of business. This minimizes the chance for someone
to inadvertently see the Due Guard and Sign on camera. However, a Lodge
would need to be careful to ensure that no other brother is shown on camera.
Transmission of any other portions of the meeting, including the opening and
closing ritual or election of officers, would not be permitted.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

255

Only Masons of the Lodge would be permitted to attend virtually. Members
of the Lodge would be permitted to vote virtually on items that require a voice
vote or the raising of hands, but no virtual balloting would be permitted. Thus,
balloting on membership and affiliations would be limited to the members
attending in person. Quorum would still be determined by the number of
members attending in person. And any Mason participating virtually would
not be permitted to fill any Lodge officer, place, or station.
An issue inherent of virtual meetings is the potential for cowans and eavesdroppers. While most of the business that would be permitted under this recommendation is not confidential, the reading of an application for membership
or affiliation includes personally identifiable information that is not normally
shared outside a tiled meeting. If this recommendation is adopted, further
guidance may be necessary to protect the privacy of applicants.
This recommendation would create an option, not a requirement, and
would affect only Stated Meetings.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek
David Doan
Peter Ackeret, Chairman

Recommendation No. 4
The intent of this recommendation is to ensure that a brother accused of
unmasonic conduct is not subject to charges on the same facts at a later date or
“double jeopardy” if he is party to a mediated settlement agreement that meets
certain conditions. It does not change the mediation process under the CMC.
Under the current provisions of the CMC, double jeopardy protection is
not afforded to an Accused that enters into a settlement agreement resulting
from any form of mediation. If this recommendation is approved, double jeopardy protection would be afforded to an Accused that enters into a settlement
agreement at mediation subject to the following conditions:
1.

The settlement agreement is in writing, signed by the Accused, the
Accuser(s), and the Trial Master;

256

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

2.

The settlement agreement includes a summary of the facts and reasoning supporting the withdrawal of the charges;

3.

The Grand Master has ordered that double jeopardy protection be
afforded; and

4.

The Committee on Trial Review has given its concurrence (which
includes reporting to and obtaining the approval of Grand Lodge at
the Annual Communication).

Double jeopardy protection would not be afforded to any other mediated
settlement agreements, including settlement agreements reached by way of
a mediation prior to the appointment of a Trial Master. If double jeopardy
protection is afforded to a mediated settlement agreement, such protection
would make those agreements not only binding on the parties, but also a final
resolution on the charges such that no Mason (whether or not party to the settlement agreement) would thereafter be able to pursue charges of unmasonic
conduct on the same facts. The CMC already provides a means for an Accused
to receive this form of double jeopardy protection when the dispute is settled
by way of a trial.
As previously noted by this committee regarding the use of mediations
generally, implementation issues will need to be addressed if this recommendation is approved. In particular, policies, procedures, and a standardized
form for settlement agreements that include sufficient information and other
requirements needed for the Grand Master and the Committee on Trial Review
to evaluate whether to afford double jeopardy protection to a mediated settlement agreement will need to be created. It should also be noted that the
CMC permits charges of unmasonic conduct against an individual Mason to be
preferred by any brother with knowledge of the facts. As a result, if this Grand
Lodge believes that it is appropriate for these mediated settlement agreements
to be final resolutions of the relevant charges as the Grand Master recommends,
this change to the CMC would be necessary to effectuate that intent.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek
David Doan
Peter Ackeret, Chairman

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

257

Recommendation No. 5
This recommendation would amend two sections of the California Masonic
Code to create the penalty of transfer of membership from the Accused brother’s
Lodge(s) to the Grand Master’s Lodge to those penalties that a Trial Master
may choose from when an Accused brother is found guilty of unmasonic conduct. Currently, voluntary demits are being used during mediations to resolve
conflicts in Lodges.
There has not been any previous legislation before Grand Lodge that proposed the creation of this penalty. The penalty of transfer of membership would
be one of lowest penalties available to the Trial Master, on par with reprimand
in open Lodge. The Trial Master would have to make a finding that the brother’s continued membership in one or more Lodges was not in the best interest
of the Craft and set the penalty as transfer of membership. If the Accused
belongs to more than one Lodge and the Trial Master does not transfer all of
his memberships, then the Accused would remain a member of those other
Lodges and not be placed in the Grand Master’s Lodge. As with all trials, the
finding of guilt and the suitability of the penalty would have to be approved by
the Grand Lodge at an Annual Communication.
A brother who has his membership transferred to the Grand Master’s
Lodge would retain all of the rights and privileges of membership in California.
The recommendation does not speak to the issue of the transferred brother
trying to attend the Lodge from which he was removed. However, he would
be a visitor and CMC section 808.040 authorizes the Master to deny entry. He
would pay dues to the Grand Master’s Lodge as long as he remains a member.
It would be up to him to find another regular Lodge and apply for affiliation.
He could even apply to his former Lodge for affiliation, but it would be subject
to a ballot by its members.
Peace and harmony in our Lodges and among our brothers is an essential
part of our brotherhood. This recommendation would add a useful tool to the
penalties available to a Trial Master after a finding of guilt. Its use would be
subject to Grand Lodge review and your approval at an Annual Communication.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria

Carryover 2019 Resolutions
Resolution 19-07
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California Masonic
Code, sections 802.020 and 807.000 to allow a Lodge to amend its bylaws to
hold Stated Meetings as few as four times a year.
The proponents state that other jurisdictions, including the United Grand
Lodge of England and some in the United States, have less-than-monthly meetings, and that system works well for them. They also feel individual Lodges
should have as much flexibility as possible.
CMC sections 805.220 and 805.230 require a Lodge to receive annual reports
from the Treasurer and Secretary in February and semiannual reports in August.
Sections 805.410 and 809.510 also require a Lodge to hold the election of officers in November and to adopt a budget no later than January. While a budget
could be adopted prior to January, perhaps in November, the requirement of
the reports from the Secretary and Treasurer and election of officers would
require meetings in February, August, and November. Depending upon the
number of bills to be paid, some Lodges may not be able to meet fewer than
12 times annually.
If adopted, this proposal would have the potential to tempt struggling
Lodges to reduce the number of their meetings for convenience, and that could
be problematic for some of them. There is value in having monthly Stated
Meetings, as it helps reinforce friendships and encourages good fellowship.
A struggling Lodge would be authorized to reduce the number of its Stated
Meetings, and that could create additional difficulties.
On the other hand, this proposal may be beneficial for some existing Lodges
and those wanting to create new Lodges. Some rural Lodges have limited memberships and have difficulty meeting monthly. Other Lodges may not have a
business need to meet monthly or may want to repurpose meeting nights for
other Masonic activities.
Adoption of this proposal would be a significant change to the CMC and
how Lodges operate in California. If adopted, this resolution has the potential
to be beneficial to some Lodges and detrimental to others.

260

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Respectfully Submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek
David Doan
Peter Ackeret, Chairman
Resolution 19-08
California Masonic Code section 809.360 currently allows a Lodge to remit
the dues of a brother who is unable to pay his dues for the current calendar
year. Proponents of this legislation seek to allow a Lodge to remit a portion of
dues owed by a brother, allowing a brother to pay what he is able towards his
dues for the year.
Proponents assert that brothers take pride in paying their dues, and for
some, being unable to pay for a given year lowers their sense of dignity. A brother
facing hardship may feel less embarrassed if he could pay at least some of his
dues. This resolution would also benefit Lodges financially because a Lodge
would receive some dues from its members that would otherwise be forfeited
if remitted in whole. The Lodge would be charged per capita only on the percentage of dues it receives from the brother.
While this resolution would result in some brothers who are in need paying
less than others during a given year, the partial remission of dues would remain
anonymous through the Lodge’s charity committee.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek
David Doan
Peter Ackeret, Chairman
Resolution 19-09
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify California Masonic Code
section 407.065 by clarifying the process of reimbursements authorized under
this section. Currently, after the close of each Annual Communication, the Grand
Lodge automatically reimburses certain travel expenses to each constituent

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Lodge in attendance, provided they have paid their per capita. If adopted, this

It should be noted that the reimbursement benefit for each Constituent

a form would need to be submitted on or before 30 days following the conclusion
of such Annual Communication to facilitate reimbursement.
It is a standard and accepted practice of business entities across all disciplines to require proper verifiable expenses before the accounting department
will issue a reimbursement check. The manner of verification may require
itemized expenses or a signed affidavit attesting to the expenses before a check
is issued. This resolution will assist our Grand Lodge Accounting Department
to resolve any potential legal issues that may arise, as well as the expeditious
processing, balancing, and reconciliation of expenses associated with section

Resolution 20-03
The proponents of this resolution seek to amend section 1404.210 of the
California Masonic Code to require three Master Masons in good standing to file
charges of unmasonic conduct. The proponents contend that the adoption of
this resolution would reduce the number of frivolous charges.
Pursuant to section 1402.210 of the CMC, charges of unmasonic conduct
may currently be brought by a single Master Mason in good standing. Section
1404.220 also requires the Junior Warden of a Lodge to investigate possible
unmasonic conduct brought to his attention and obligates him to file charges if
he has reasonable cause to believe that a Mason is guilty of unmasonic conduct.
While this resolution would require three Master Masons in good standing to
bring charges under section 1402.210, it would make no changes to the duties

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

263

and process for charges brought by a Junior Warden under section 1404.220.
The quality of charges of unmasonic conduct is a continued concern of
this Grand Lodge. Recent attempts to address this issue includes Grand Master
Nagel’s Recommendation 3 in 2010, which added section 1404.315 of the CMC to
require the Committee on Jurisprudence to review all charges for proper form.
That section was amended in 2013 by Resolution 13-16 to also require a review
for content and allow dismissal in certain circumstances.
Pursuing charges that lack reasonable cause have negative consequences.
They tend to create disharmony in affected Lodges. They also consume the
limited resources available for the investigation and trial procedures required
by the CMC: Specifically, qualified Trial Masters, Commissioners, and counsel
are in limited supply.
Requiring three Master Masons to concur in the filing of charges would
likely mitigate abuse in the filing of charges in furtherance of personal disputes.
It is reasonable to believe that any malfeasance severe enough to meet the
threshold of unmasonic conduct would likely persuade three Master Masons
to concur in filing charges. It is also possible that genuine unmasonic conduct
could be witnessed by only one Master Mason. But in such a situation, that
single Master Mason could notify the Junior Warden and seek to have charges
brought under section 1404.220.
While this resolution would likely reduce the number of charges filed
without reasonable cause, it could also prevent meritorious charges from being
filed. It is the prerogative of this Grand Lodge to weigh the likelihood of benefit
against the risk of harm.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge
David Ferreria
Chris Holme
Steven Wolvek
David Doan
Peter Ackeret, Chairman

Resolutions for 2021

Resolution 21-01
This resolution seeks to require the Master to deliver an admonition against
disharmony before the Lodge is formally opened. This admonition would be
given before the Junior Deacon invites the brethren into the Lodge.
Currently, no such admonition is required before the opening of a Lodge.
However, the Master reminds the brethren to conduct themselves with due
order and propriety as part of the opening.
Protecting Lodge autonomy has been important to this Grand Lodge since
its formation. Some practices are beneficial for some Lodges and not others.
Mandating practices has typically arisen from legal requirements or a compelling
reason. While there is no legal reason for requiring every Lodge to deliver such
an admonition, there may be a compelling one.
It may not be possible to predict or quantify the impact this resolution
would actually have, if adopted. However, here are some pertinent considerations. Some Lodges may not need this admonition and may feel this added
requirement is an unneeded infringement on their autonomy. Some Lodges may
well benefit from this admonition, but would not give it if it were optional. For
those Lodges, even if the admonition were mandatory, it may still fall on deaf
ears. And for those Lodges who think they would not benefit from it, maybe
they would, and maybe they are at risk of piques and quarrels overflowing from
other Lodges.
Respectfully submitted,
Vern Dandridge

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON TRIAL REVIEW
2020–21 MASONIC YEAR
Your Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records of
only two matters this year, due to decreased referrals resulting from the COVID19 pandemic. There are additional cases pending.
In Case Number 2876, the Accused was charged with an attempted criminal act of lewd and lascivious conduct with a child. A YouTube video taken by
non-Masons was posted online recording a series of text and chat messages
between the Accused and a person who identified himself as a 14-year-old male.
These documented communications exhibited the Accused offering an
exchange of sexual acts and the arranging of a physical meeting to engage in such
acts. The video further showed the Accused’s arrival at the intended meeting
location, where the Accused was confronted by members of a non-Masonic
undercover community group whose mission is to expose and discourage adults
seeking to engage in sexual conduct with minors.
The video was presented as evidence at the pretrial conference held by the
Trial Master. Although the Accused initially pled not guilty, he subsequently,
prior to trial, revised his response to a plea of guilty. The Trial Master investigated and found the Accused guilty of unmasonic conduct and set the penalty
at expulsion.
The Trial Review Committee determined there was compliance with the
procedural requirements of the California Masonic Code and that the findings
of fact and penalty were supported by the evidence.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the adoption of the following resolution: Resolved, that in case number 2876 the
Trial Master’s proceedings, findings, and penalty affixed be hereby affixed.
Case Number 2738 is the third request by the applicant for restoration. At
trial, the Trial Master, despite the Accused’s denial of the offense, found the
Accused, while acting as a Steward, struck the hoodwinked candidate in the
preparation room.
On this third attempt, the Accused has now taken responsibility for the

266

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

act, its seriousness and damage to the fraternity, and expressed remorse. He
has apologized in writing to the candidate, who provided his forgiveness in
writing. These elements as required by Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No.
3 had not been included in prior restoration requests.
The applicant has been out of Masonry for six years, and it appears he has
learned that this type of conduct will not be tolerated. A large plurality of his
lodge is ready to receive him as an active member.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following resolution: Resolved, that in case number 2738,
the application for restoration be granted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Arthur Weiss, and the members of the Grand
Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:
The world has thrust upon us challenges that few have ever encountered. This upheaval has been manifested even more among our youth. The
global pandemic has turned their educations and socialization upside down.
The long-term effects may not be known for years.
Yet through it all, our Masonic youth orders have served as anchors in
these tumultuous seas.
Fortunately, California Freemasonry has long realized that by investing
in the development and growth of our three Masonic youth orders (Job’s
Daughters, Rainbow for Girls, and DeMolay), we are repairing our world.
Your Grand Lodge Committee on Youth Orders is charged with ensuring
that our lodges and members continue to support our youth orders by providing
the necessary leadership and assistance to aid in their success.
Having accomplished much of our previous strategic plan, we revised our
direction to focus on:
• Creating awareness of and providing education about our three
Masonic youth orders
• Serving as a liaison between our youth orders and Masonry
• Building the bond between our youth orders and Masonry.
In order to accomplish these objectives, we have divided the committee into
sub-committees. These teams work behind the scenes and in between our
meetings to fulfill our objectives.
You can expect to receive frequent updates on what our youth orders are
doing and, more importantly, how you can support them; as it is only with your
support and guidance that our youth will become the future on which we are
all counting.
We continue to coordinate with the Masonic Center for Youth and Families
to identify our youth in need and to stretch forth a helping hand. Especially
during this difficult period when we all miss in-person connections, we are

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CALIFORNIA FREEMASON MAGAZINE
The California Freemason Magazine Committee provides guidance
and feedback to, and offers editorial direction and brainstorming for, the staff
of California Freemason, the flagship publication of the Masons of California.
In 2020–21, the magazine was redesigned to better reflect the organization’s
strategy of highlighting more Masons and appealing to a younger audience, the
fastest-growing segment of the Fraternity. Most visibly, the redesign involved
the development of the Mosaic, a diverse range of topical, short-form stories
about Masons and Masonry today. This effort was recognized with a gold award
at the annual Association Media and Publishing conference for best redesign.
Not only does this redesign appeal more broadly to our target audiences, but
the stories in this section are more appealing to new audiences and those
curious about who and what Masonry is today. The magazine also received a
bronze award for its Spring 2020 issue devoted to Masonic relief in the time of
COVID-19 and unprecedented wildfires.
In addition to the redesign, the magazine saw several other changes in the
past year: The publication shifted to a longer format (typically 48 pages) and
adopted a quarterly print schedule, both of which allow it to dive deeper into
rich topics and themes. As the magazine has shifted its focus away from issues
related solely to the Craft itself and toward highlighting members and the way
their lives interact with Freemasonry, there has been a renewed emphasis on
high-quality photography. As a result of these changes, the Grand Lodge communications team ended their partnership with their longtime design and print
partner, bringing photography and design responsibilities in-house for the first
time and partnering with a new printing press. This change was long overdue,
and already the quality of both the design and the printing has been elevated,
changes we expect the magazine’s readership to see and feel.
This shift in tone and substance was reflected in the editorial themes the
magazine pursued in 2020–21: A future-themed issue spotlighting the next
generation of Masonic leaders remaking the Craft in their image (Winter 2020);
a first-ever drinks issue that dives into the tradition of Masonic refreshment
(Spring 2021); a study of Filipino Masonic culture in California and beyond
(Summer 2021); and, finally, the Bridge Builders issue, devoted to the concept
of Masonic harmony that is the cornerstone of the Fraternity (Fall 2021).
On the digital publication side, this year marked the first year to offer free
digital subscriptions to the general public. Subscriptions quickly numbered in

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

271

the hundreds and continue to climb with each additional issue. The magazine
has also begun to dabble in digital events related to issue launches. The first
of these, which corresponded to the spring drinks issue, involved bringing
together a Mason and champagne expert with Grand Master Arthur Weiss over
Facebook Live, which was viewed by more than 1,200 people—a modest but
promising starting point.
The Grand Lodge of California is an exemplar among Masonic jurisdictions
in the world; fittingly, our signature publication will continue to reflect—and
push—that leadership into the future.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Editor in Chief
Arthur H. Weiss, Grand Master
